DISTRICT PRIMARY EDUCATION PROGRAMME
Observation/Recommendation
7.1       The District Primary Education Programme was launched in 1994, as a major initiative to revitalize the primary
education system and to achieve the objective of universalisation of primary education.  It is a Centrally- sponsored
scheme with the Central Govt. contributing 85 per cent of the project cost and the State Governments contributing the
remaining 15 per cent.  The Central Government's contribution is resourced entirely through external funding.  17
districts of Bihar, 8 districts of Orissa, 56 districts of UP and 34 districts of MP are covered under  DPEP.   The
Committee was given to understand that the norms prescribed by the World Bank with regard to school buildings are
not flexible. The Committee desires that it  may be reviewed.
Action Taken
The World Bank and other funding agencies have not prescribed any norms for construction of school buildings.  The
design, specification etc. are decided by the project implementing agencies depending on the area of construction. Under
the DPEP guidelines, which were formulated with the approval of the Cabinet, the ceiling on civil works was prescribed
at 24% of the project cost. Keeping in view the demand from States, the ceiling has already been increased to 33%.
Since, for achieving the objective of universalisation of elementary education, other components like appointment of
additional teachers, teacher training, curriculum development, academic resource support, community mobilisation etc.
are also important, the above ceiling has been considered to be reasonable to keep the balance between the various
components. In fact, under the scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, the same ceiling for civil works has been fixed.
 Observation/Recommendation
7.2       Committee’s attention has been drawn to the Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year
ending March, 2000 (No. 3 of 2001).  Audit has reviewed the DPEP in 70 districts of 14 States including Bihar, Orissa,
MP and UP, covering the period from 1994-1995 to 1999-2000, during the period from October 1999 to July 2000. 
Major findings of the audit with special reference to these four States can be listed as follows:-
(a) UNDERUTILIZATION OF EXTERNAL AID
              Audit observed that the disbursements pledged by the funding agencies could not be utilised optimally.  For
DPEP Phase III Bihar, against its target of US Dollar 65.25 million, upto 31
st March 2000, IDA released only US
Dollars 16.448 million.  Reason attributed is low pace of expenditure.
Action Taken
The major reasons for low expenditure and consequent low disbursement under DPEP-III Bihar is non-filling up of

132ReportofHRD

various posts including  teachers  by the State Government and time taken in sorting out contractual problems with the
Bihar State Textbook Publishing Corporation for printing and supply of textbooks. Disbursement in foreign exchange
has also been less than the targets due to exchange rate variations. The project is being restructured in consultation with
the World Bank and the proposal also includes extension of the project period by 2 years i.e. upto 30/9/2005 to ensure
full utilisation of committed external assistance and to achieve the planned targets.
JANSHALA PROGRAMME
Observation/Recommendation
8.3       The Committee is of the view that the  Scheme is in the initial stages of implementation and needs more time to
get the actual feedback about the scheme.  The Committee, however,  hopes that the observations made in the report of
the Bodh Shiksha Samiti will  help the Government in formulating its future strategy in regard to the Scheme. 
Action Taken
8.3       The report of the Bodh Shiksha Samiti has been circulated to all the programme States with direction to
formulate appropriate strategy for improving the classroom practices. All the States  have taken steps in this direction
through teacher training programmes and introduction of improved teaching-learning methods.
EDUCATION OF SC/ST CHILDREN
Observation/Recommendation
12.5     The Committee notes the ambitious interventions of the Government which have now become part of Sarva
Shiksha Abhiyan.  Since the SSA is still in initial stage of its implementation, the Committee can only hope that these
efforts will yield the desired result.  However, the Committee recommends accordingly that  such blocks/districts where
the tribal women literacy (as in the case of Orissa where it is merely 1.8%) is much below should be identified and
given special attention in the implementation of the scheme.
Action Taken
With a view to improving the position of girls education, it is also envisaged to provide additional inputs in the form of
various incentives and interventions like supply of free textbooks, uniforms, transport subsidy,  setting up of model
cluster schools, community mobilisation etc. by making suitable amendments in the scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan.
An amount of Rs. 1,000 crores has been earmarked within the allocation of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan for additional 
interventions for promoting girls education in the 2198 educationally backward blocks where female literacy is lower
than the national average.
 CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE
IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
ENROLMENT & DROPOUT
Observation/Recommendation
3.3       The Committee feels that one of the major reasons is the lack of facilities in the habitations where there is no
provision for encouragement to study.  The teachers are also not attending the schools regularly.  The presence of the
education centre at a far off place from the scattered habitation is also not motivating the children from that area to
continue study.  In rural areas, the children are still helping their parents in farming and other household work for their
livelihood, which is discouraging them to attend the classes regularly.  In order to address these issues, necessary
provisions have to be made to open the schools in the vicinity of the scattered habitations, which has not been done. The
Committee observes that lack/absence of infrastructure and lack of motivation in teachers can be cited as the other main
reasons for high rate of drop out.  Besides all this, the economic factor, which is responsible to a great extent for this
continuing problem, has to be effectively dealt with through various incentives/ encouragement to needy and poor
children,  all of which are long pending. 
Action Taken
Agreeing to the observations of the Committee, it is stated that Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) provides for opening of
primary schools/EGS centres in all habitations where there is no schooling facility within 1 km. There is also provision
of teacher training and free textbooks to provide for better quality of education. Free textbooks and midday meal is
being provided as incentives to the children.
OPERATION BLACKBOARD
Observation/Recommendation
4.3       The Committee  observes that except U.P. none of the three States has been able to achieve the physical targets 
relating to construction of classrooms under the Scheme.    The States of Bihar, M.P. and Orissa have remained far away

132ReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report132th.htm[01-07-2016 16:10:53]
from achievement of the target.   The Committee would also like to point out that these targets are based on the
requirement of classrooms in  1986.   Since  then, requirement of classrooms should  have increased manifold.   The
Committee is therefore, of the view that progress in construction of classrooms should be regularly monitored.
Action Taken
The scheme of Operation Blackboard, inter-alia, envisaged the provision of two reasonably large rooms, which
are usable in all weather with a deep veranda along with separate toilet facilities for boys and girls.  However, no
separate funds were being provided under OB by Ministry of HRD (Dept of Education) for construction of
primary school building.  Provision for this component of school building was made under the programmes of
Rural Employment like JRY and EAS.
As regards increase in the requirement of classrooms, the District Primary Education Programme (DPEP) and Sarva
Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) have provisions for meeting the additional requirements of classrooms.  There is an inbuilt
mechanism in these schemes/programmes for monitoring the achievements of civil works.
Observation/Recommendation
4.13     The Committee also noted instances of absenteeism of teachers or no teacher- in- charge of the schools during its
visits. The Committee finds such a situation very disturbing and unhealthy and is constrained to observe  that the
Department needs to take this matter very seriously with the concerned State Governments and impress upon them to
effectively deal with this unhealthy  situation in the interest of the students and also for prudent  expenditure of
Government funds.
Action Taken
The Department had been impressing upon the States from time to time to rationalize the deployment of teachers
in such a away that every primary school has at least two teachers, one of them should be a woman.  Further, the
Department has also been emphasizing that the replacement should be provided immediately if a teacher
appointed under OB is transferred to another school.
Under the SSA, States Governments have been advised to decentralize powers for appointment of teachers and their
posting in order to address this situation.
In Madhya Pradesh, the posting of teachers is being rationalised at the district level and the district planning committee
has been given the powers to take decision on rationalisation .The new policy of recruitment of contract teachers
envisages school specific posting of teachers and the services are non-transferable.  This has helped considerably in
eliminating the teacher absenteeism. Village Education Committees (VEC) in all the primary schools of the state have
been given powers to monitor teacher attendance in schools and with the activation of VEC there is visible increased
supervision and monitoring and reduction in teacher absenteeism.
In Uttar Pradesh, the State Government has issued orders for rationalization of teacher deployment.  It has banned any
transfers from rural areas to urban schools and has insisted on redeployment of existing teachers as per sanctioned
school strength.  Shiksha Mitras are appointed in a ratio of 2:3 with regular teachers, which in itself effects a
rationalization in the deployment of regular Assistant Teachers apart from improving the Teacher-pupil ratio.
In Bihar, teacher’s attendance is being monitored by Village Education Committees/Panchyati Raj Institutions.
In Orissa, Community supervision through School Committee (VEC) have reduced the incidence of teacher
absenteeism in DPEP districts.  Combined with this, administrative actions have been initiated against several truant
teachers.
NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT TO PRIMARY EDUCATION (MID-DAY
MEAL SCHEME)
Observation/Recommendation
6.3       The Committee observes that situation is highly discouraging and disappointing in Bihar.  Out of the 57 districts
of undivided Bihar, in 15 districts there has been no lifting of foodgrains since 1998-99, in 26 districts no foodgrain has
been allocated since 1999-2000.  In the remaining districts also, lifting of foodgrains has been far below the allocated 
foodgrains. What is a cause of serious concern is that even these lifting figures furnished by the State Govt. do not
match with the off take figures furnished by the FCI.  The Committee finds that in Orissa, a declining trend is there in

result that there is nobody to take responsibility for sending reports from districts to States and States to Centre.  The
Committee takes a serious view of this. The Committee is also of the opinion that provision of foodgrains instead of
cooked meals defeats the very purpose of the scheme.
Action Taken

With regard to requirement of reasonable staff for smooth implementation of the scheme it is submitted that Ministry of

However, this Ministry has not been given any additional funds to support the States for putting in place a cooked meal

DISTRICT PRIMARY EDUCATION PROGRAMME
Observation/Recommendation
7.2 (C) ACCESS TO EDUCATIONAL FACILITIES
Status of infrastructure facilities under DPEP scheme during 1999-2000 as emerging in the data compiled by
Educational Consultants India Ltd in respect of Bihar, Orissa, M.P. and U.P. is as follows:
 
Action Taken
The District Primary Education Programme (DPEP) has been planned to provide only additional inputs over and above
other schemes in the State and Central Sectors for elementary education. The school infrastructure situation in most of
the project districts was very poor prior to the implementation of DPEP. As a result all districts had a huge infrastructure
gap to be filled up within limited funds. In the prioritization exercise that followed, school buildings in school less
habitations, buildingless schools and additional classrooms received a higher priority because of their direct influence
on access and retention. It was, therefore, not possible to bridge the entire infrastructure gap in the district only through
DPEP funds and gaps with regard to toilets, drinking water, repairs and additional classrooms therefore  still remain in
most districts. Under the financial parameters of the DPEP, there was a ceiling of 24% expenditure on civil works,
which has now been raised to 33-1/3%. Under DPEP, the position of new school buildings, additional classrooms and
toilets constructed/in progress upto 31.03.2002 in the concerned four states is as follows:
 
State School Buildings Addl. Class rooms Textiles
Bihar 658 1114 1035
M.P. 16550 4548 0
Orissa 990 778 1240
 
In Madhya Pradesh, construction of toilets is included in the school buildings or taken up under other schemes.
Convergence has been attempted  at the National level with the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission to
address the issue of  water and sanitation in a more holistic way. Efforts would also be to fill in the remaining gaps
under the scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA).
Observation/Recommendation
7.2 (E)   MONITORING AT THE CENTRAL LEVEL
At the Central level, the General Council was required to meet annually and the Project Board quarterly to monitor the
progress.  It was noticed that at the national level, during the review period (1994-2000) only one meeting of the
General Council was held in November 1997 and the Project Board held only seven meetings.

132ReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report132th.htm[01-07-2016 16:10:53]
Action Taken
The Project Board meetings at the National level and the Executive Committee meetings of the DPEP Societies are
generally held regularly.  At the  national level,  efforts   will be made to  hold the next General Council Meeting at the
earliest.  States have also been advised to hold meetings of the General Body regularly. However, at national level,
officers and Consultants visit States and Districts at regular intervals and prepare reports on various components of
programme implementation. Similarly officers and Consultants from the project State visit blocks and districts
regularly.  Most of the States have developed indicators and formats to review and monitor the progress of the
programme implementation in blocks and districts.  The progress of the programme is also reviewed and monitored in
the quarterly Executive Committee meetings and the Governing Body meetings of the DPEP State Societies.  Internal
Supervision Missions (ISM) are launched as targeted missions for specific purposes as and when required.
JANSHALA PROGRAMME
Observation/Recommendation
8.4       The Committee observes that implementation of the Scheme  in all the above States is very slow and urgent
remedial measures need to be taken by the Department as the scheme is scheduled to run for only 18 months more i.e.
upto March, 2003.
Action Taken
Though, the programme started in 1998, its actual implementation was delayed due to various reasons, such as changes

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
GOVERNMENT 
VI        POOR CONDITION OF GOVT. MEDICAL COLLEGES  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
6.1       The Committee had the opportunity to visit a number of State-run medical colleges, besides 
interacting with medical professionals associated with such colleges.  The Committee observed that 
overall condition of these medical colleges was very bad.  The Committee was given to understand that 
there had been no improvement in the infrastructure facilities  for the medical colleges established long 
time back.   Even though there has been  manifold increase in the number of undergraduate and 
postgraduate seats, the facilities remained virtually the same.    Not only this, many new  paramedical 
courses have also been started without going into the availability of basic  infrastructure.   No new 
classrooms have been added, labs have tremendous scarcity of space and classrooms were equipped with 
the minimum teaching aids.   Over the  years, what has happened is that all the modern technology 
developments have not reached such colleges and as a result both teachers and doctors are not fully 
exposed to the latest techniques.   General opinion was that there was a need for having a moratorium  
on establishing new medical colleges in States having large concentration.  Instead attention was 
required to be focuses on updating the infrastructure of existing medical colleges. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
6.2       The Committee is inclined to agree with this view-point.   The Committee  is of the view 
that there is an urgent need for undertaking a review of  infrastructure status of all state-run 
medical  colleges in the country.   Non-existence of required facilities tend to create an atmosphere 
which  has a de-motivating effect on the teachers/doctors/students.    The Committee understands 
that Central Govt. has  already launched a pilot project for providing financial assistance to some 
State Govt.  medical colleges/hospitals.   The Committee feels that a time-bound action plan for 
revamping the infrastructure facilities should be drawn by the Central Govt. which could be 
implemented by State Govts in active co-ordination with Central Govt. and MCI. 
ACTION TAKEN 
 6.1&6.2    Though the State run medical colleges are bound by the MCI Regulations on the 
requirements for a Medical College vis-à-vis the admission capacity, the facilities available in some 
of the Government Medical Colleges are in a poor state.  Presently, the Central Govt. has 
launched a pilot scheme for providing financial assistance to State Govt. Medical colleges for 
strengthening their diagnostic facilities.  
XI. TEACHERS 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
11.4     The Committee finds that in states like Maharashtra and Gujarat, shortage of faculty strength in 
Govt. medical college has been addressed to some extent by having two types of teachers -  Full-time 
and Honorary teachers.  Although divergent views were given with regard to honorary teachers, the 
Committee had a feeling that both the categories of teachers  were playing a complimentary role.   The 
Committee observes that in spite of there being a provision for only full-time teachers in MCI 
Regulations on the request of some State Govts., system of honorary teachers has been further extended 
Page 4 of 36133rdReportofHRd
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report133rd.htm

by the Central Govt.  upto 30th June, 2002.   The  Committee is of the view that Central Govt./MCI 
should undertake a detailed review of Honorary System of teachers in the concerned States.   The 
Committee is of the view that after removal of all the  loopholes in this system and also safeguarding the 
interest of Full time teachers, other State Govts. can be approached to take benefit of Honorary System 
of teachers to the extent possible.  
ACTION TAKEN 
11.4     Taking into account the dearth of experienced teachers, the Central Govt. has extended the 
system of appointment of honorary/part-time teachers in the medical institutions for a further period of 
five years i.e. October 2006. This communication has been sent to all the State Govts., Universities and 
the Heads of all medical institutions for appropriate action. The MCI is, however, of the view that the 
engagement of honorary teachers may be made only in addition to the regular teaching faculty as 
required to be provided under the Council's Regulations. 
Recommendation/Observation 
11.5     The Committee finds that the UGC guidelines regarding extension of retired medical teachers of 
all medical colleges/institutions on yearly basis upto the age of 65 years have been agreed to by the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 1997.   The Committee feels that this directive should be 
given wide publicity  so that the Govt. medical colleges may take benefit of the same.  Besides that, 
possibility of hiring the services of  medical professionals – Visiting Professors and practicing doctors 
without compromising the standard of medical education can also be explored.  
Action Taken 
11.5     The Council is of the view that the possibility of hiring the services of medical professionals, 
visiting professors and practicing doctors can be permitted only in addition to the prescribed 
requirement of full-time teachers by the regulations and without compromising the standard of medical 
education. 
XII       TRAINING 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
12.1     During its interactions, Committee’s attention was drawn time and again about there being need 
for having some kind of training for medical teachers.   The majority view was that it is not necessary 
that a good medical practitioner is also a good teacher.  The Committee observes that most postgraduate 
teaching programmes have a component of students taking classes of undergraduate courses and also  
conducting seminars as part of their training. In spite of that, it was emphasized that training to 
prospective teachers  specially for communication skills was very much required.  The Committee 
strongly feels that training in educational technology should be made the eligibility criteria for 
appointment of a medical teacher.   If that is not considered feasible, extensive training programme of 
short duration should be mandatory before   the prospective teachers join their duties.  
ACTION TAKEN 
12.1     The Council's regulations only prescribe the minimum qualification and experience to be 
possessed by the medical teachers in different specialities. While agreeing with the recommendations of 
the Committee, considering the shortage of teachers in certain specialities it is felt that the training in 
educational technology can be made compulsory for the medical teachers within a fixed time after they 
join duties. The State Governments and institutions can set up training centres for this purpose..  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
12.2     Committee’s attention was also drawn to the fact that there was also a constant need to have in-
service training programme/refresher course for doctors involved in teaching to update their knowledge 
especially during the present era when rapid scientific developments are taking place and a wide variety 
of  diseases are being recognized.   The Committee finds that Graduate Medical Education Regulations 
provide that Medical Education Units/Departments be established in all medical colleges for faculty 
development and providing learning resource material to teachers.   The Committee is, however, 
constrained to note that these directives are not being adhered to as only about 50-60 medical colleges in 
the country  have established such units so far.   The Committee is of the opinion that fulfillment of this 
condition should be pursued with all medical colleges, both Govt. and private. 
Page 5 of 36133rdReportofHRd
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report133rd.htm

ACTION TAKEN 
12.2     The Council has been taking up the matter with all the medical colleges and so far about 130 
medical colleges have intimated the functioning of such units as per the guidelines of the Council. 
XV       PROBLEM OF SHORTAGE OF DOCTORS IN RURAL AREAS – REMEDIES 
THEREFOR  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
15.4     The Committee has been given to understand that some State Govts. have  adopted the policy of 
making rural service compulsory in the initial posting of medical officers before they are transferred to 
urban areas or permitted to do postgraduate medical education.   There is no shortage  of doctors as 
such, but there is mal-distribution between the  rural and urban areas.   The Committee is of the view 
that compulsion alone will not have the desired results.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
alongwith compulsory rural service for a limited specified time, incentives like special allowance, better 
housing and other allied facilities and special relaxation for admission to postgraduate courses are also 
necessary for attracting young doctors towards rural areas. 
ACTION TAKEN 
15.4     As per the decisions arrived in the Central Council for Health & Family Welfare, the State 
Govts. have been periodically advised to take various incentive measures to attract doctors for rural 
service, such as improving infrastructure facilities for doctors to remove their hardships, making rural 
service obligatory for three years, reservation of 25% of Postgraduate medical seats in medical colleges 
for in-service candidates who have.worked in rural areas for at least three years with a bond that 
thereafter they will serve the Government for at least five years etc. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
15.6     There was also a need for developing proper infrastructure in PHCs.   The Committee is of the 
view that the Department should pursue this issue with the State Govts.  The Committee understands the 
limitations of the Centre, health being a State subject.   However, PHCs are being maintained through 
Central Grants.  Hence, the need for Central monitoring about upkeep of PHCs is also there. 
ACTION TAKEN 
15.6     Wherever schemes are running with Central grants, the Central Government is obliged to 
monitor the execution of such schemes. The recommendation of the Committee in this regard will be 
kept in view while providing grants to the PHCs.  
XX       POWERS OF UNIVERSITY/HEALTH UNIVERSITY 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
20.1     All medical colleges in the country are affiliated to one University or the other.  Besides that, the 
States of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Punjab have established Medical

institutions in health sciences. The Committee had the opportunity to  interact with the  representatives 
of some of the Universities including Health  Universities of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka 
and Maharashtra.   The major issues/problems with regard to functioning of universities/medical 
universities can be enumerated as given below :- 
Besides allopathic system, institutions of other systems of medicine being brought under the jurisdiction 
of Health University in one or two states has created procedural problems due to proper infrastructure 
not being there for the management of such a large number of  institutions. 
Resource  crunch being faced as funds being provided by State/Centre  not adequate  enough.  Need for 
having a separate Commission like UGC emphasized  for universities/health universities. 
There was no provision for setting up a Senate in a Health University.   As a result, Health Universities 
being deprived of their right of representation in MCI. 
Need for involving representative of a University/Health University in the exercise of 
formulation/revision of curriculum for medical education related courses. 
Only exam-holding powers vested with University/Health University. Local University should also be 
involved in the exercise of opening of new colleges/increasing the intake capacity/starting of new course 
alongwith MCI/Central Govt.

Effective involvement of local universities in the inspection of medical colleges.

RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
23.1     The Committee had very fruitful discussions with representatives of student community of all the 
medical colleges visited by it.   Various suggestions for improvement of medical education based on 
their experience were put forth before the Committee which are reflected in the Report.  Besides that, 
the students also drew the attention of the Committee to a number of problems being faced by them 
which are enumerated below :- 
Due to a prolonged admission procedure for MBBS, session for 1st year generally starts very late. 
Maximum publicity needs to be  given to the rules/regulations and conditions with respect to admission 
procedure for the convenience of students.

Hostel accommodation satisfying the needs of entire student community not there.   Majority of the

RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
24.1     There has been gradual erosion in the traditional relations between students and teachers in

intake capacity and introduction of a new or higher course of study  has  checked  the mushroom growth 
of  medical colleges in the country to some extent.   However, these norms need to be enforced

functioning of both govt. and  private  medical colleges was also received from different quarters.   
While it is true that  common parameters about the  two categories of medical colleges can not be drawn,

barely reach the standards and  norms set up by MCI  with regard to infrastructure, manpower etc.

lacking.

RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION

IX        EXAMINATION PROCEDURE 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
9.1       MCI Regulations on Graduate Medical  Education, 1997 deal extensively with the examination 
procedure to be followed for obtaining MBBS degree.   Attendance, internal assessment and university 
examinations are the three basic factors on which performance of a student in essential components of 
training is to be assessed.   Detailed procedure for internal assessment and conducting university 
examination has been laid down.   Distribution of marks to various disciplines has also been specified.   
Criteria for appointment of examiners – both external and internal -  is   also there.   There is a separate 
chapter on ‘Internship’ outlining beside other aspects the specific objectives, distribution of compulsory 
and elective posting in various disciplines and the methodology for assessment of internship etc.    Even 
model time-table for different semesters has been given. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
9.2       During the course of its discussions with various authorities, the Committee had the opportunity 
to hear divergent views on various aspects of examination procedure for MBBS course.   Semester 
system was generally welcomed.   However,  there were views both in favour and against internal 
assessment.  One view was that internal assessment of students should be given due weightage as it 
would result in improved attendance.  However, apprehensions were also there as it was felt that element 
of partiality was bound to be there in internal assessment.   It was also pointed out that examiners were 
not being appointed as per MCI norms.   Views were also expressed both for and against multiple choice 
system in question papers. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
9.3       The Committee is of the view that MCI norms are not being strictly adhered to by many of the 
medical colleges.   Had it been so, there would not have been such reservations and also variations in 
examination patterns being followed by different institutions/universities.  The Committee would also 
like to point out that uniformity of examination pattern to the maximum extent possible can only be   
achieved if the teaching facilities and  courses are also uniform.  The Committee, therefore, is of the

view that steps need to be initiated for evolving a forum for interaction amongst medical faculties of 
different universities on this aspect of medical education.

9.1to9.3           The concept of uniformity in curriculum, required hours of teaching and training and 
scheme of examination has been achieved significantly through incorporation in the Regulations on 
Graduate Medical Education.  However, the Council has always provided a national forum for

workshops periodically and implementing recommendations emanating therefrom.

possible service conditions to the medical teachers.   Their pay scales and other incentives need to be of

RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
14.1     The issue of private practice by medical college teachers was raised time and again during the 
deliberations of the Committee with all categories of medical professionals – doctors, teachers, state 
authorities, student community.   Besides that, the Committee also received lot of feedback on this issue 
from various parts of the country.   The Committee observes that at present, no uniform system with 
regard to private practice by teachers is prevailing in the various medical colleges.   There are colleges 
where teachers of clinical subjects  are allowed to do private practice and teachers of non-clinical 
subjects are eligible for non-practicing allowance.   Besides that, in some states, there is a total ban on 
private practice by medical teachers.    Instances are also there of teachers, in spite of  getting NPA,

all teachers should be full-time in medical  colleges and attached hospitals.   The Committee has been

grant of NPA to medical staff  including the teachers and have abolished private practice. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
14.3     The Committee strongly feels that the teaching institutions should have non-practicing staff.   
Private practice wherever in vogue is largely affecting the quality of functioning of the Institute as well

as proper patient care  because teachers are more interested in private practice rather than in imparting

their profession.   The Committee has been given to understand that the varying rates of NPA are 
prevalent in different State Govt. medical colleges which are less than Central Govt. rates.  The

III      MEDICAL COUNCIL OF INDIA 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.5       In some states, a number of Universities now fall under the jurisdiction of Health Universities  
established in the recent years.   This development has led to a peculiar situation.   By virtue of coming 
under the jurisdiction of a Health University, such Universities   have lost their right of being 
represented in the Council.   On the other hand, Health Universities  cannot send their nominee to the  
Council as they do not have any Senate.   Thus, as many as 21 Universities over and above 56 eligible 
Universities are not represented in the Council.   Health Universities   having a  large number of medical 
colleges under their  jurisdiction, specially  in southern  and western states have no say in the decision-
making apex body on medical education. 
ACTION TAKEN

entitled to send one member to the Council and this provision is also available to the Health Universities 
set up in some of the States.   
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee is  aware of the provision of Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, which lays down 
that any University having a medical faculty is entitled to send one member to the Council.   
However, the problem is that some Universities are still un-represented  in the Medical Council as 
they do not have a Senate in existence.   In view of this, the Committee recommends that sincere 
efforts be made for the constitution of 'Senate' in such Universities so as to enable them to be  
represented in the Indian Medical Council. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.11     The Committee is not inclined to agree with the viewpoint  of the Council.  In its all the study 
visits  and interactions with the various   functionaries comprising the entire medical education   
spectrum, one view  that has been consistently put across before the Committee, was that with the 
increase  in the number of medical colleges over the years, it is practically not possible for a centralized 
body like MCI to constantly monitor the standard of medical education.    The Committee observes that 
there is no regional council of the MCI.   The State  Medical Councils are autonomous bodies 
established by State Govts that too not by all the State Govts.    These  State Medical Councils have no   
authority in the maintenance of standards of medical education.   In such a  scenario with 183   medical 
colleges spread across the country with chances  of future expansion, the Committee strongly feels that 
regional  councils  with MCI continuing as the apex body need to be set up in the country.   The 
Committee is of the view that, both the Central Govt. and MCI should explore the possibility of setting 
up four regional councils  in  Southern, Northern, Eastern and Western parts of the country.   This would 
ultimately lead to better monitoring of the standard of medical  education as laid down in the IMC Act, 
1956,  and regulations made thereunder.     The Committee also desires that the Department may take up 
the matter of establishing  State Medical Council in the States where they are not existing.   Role of 
State Medical Council may also be reviewed so as to involve them in the exercise of maintaining the

standards of Medical Education in the States under the guidance of MCI. 
ACTION TAKEN 
3.11     The Medical Council of India has proposed that there is more of a need to strengthen the Council 
with more regulatory authority through appropriate amendments in the Act.  Setting up of zonal 
branches of the Medical Council of India is something to be viewed from the administrative feasibility 
and the financial constraints.  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee notes that the Medical Council of India has proposed  appropriate  amendments 
in the Act for the purpose  of strengthening the Council with more regulatory authority. The 
Committee, however, feels that empowering the Council alone will not remedy the situation, as 
monitoring of the standards of Medical Education by State-run Medical colleges/universities has 
to be done from close quarters.   The Committee, reiterates its recommendation that despite the  
administrative and financial constraints, the possibility of setting up four regional councils in 
Southern, Northern, Eastern and Western parts of the country should be explored simultaneously 
by both the Central Government and the Medical Council of India.  The Department should take 
up the establishment of State Medical Councils in the States where they are not presently existing, 
besides reviewing their role.  
V.  INSPECTION 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
5.4        The Committee notes that a number of steps  have been taken by MCI to make the procedure of 
inspection foolproof.   For example, the medical colleges are now supposed to maintain a list of teachers 
on their strength  alongwith their photographs  duly verified by the Dean of the College. The Committee, 
however, is of the view that there is a need for  streamlining the inspection procedure so as to make it 
more stringent and effective.  The Committee understands that, so far, inspections are being carried out 
only  after giving prior  notice.   The Committee is of the view that MCI should initiate measures  so as 
to build up  a  mechanism for carrying out surprise inspections and inspections at a very short notice.   
This would indirectly lead to a  situation where medical college authorities would work towards having 
a proper set up as per the prescribed norms.   The Committee is also of  the view that rate  of fees 
charged  for different  categories of inspection should be reviewed.   Specially, in spite of   the so-called 
annual inspections being  carried out only once in five years,  annual fee of Rs. 30,000 is prescribed  
which  seems to be on the high side. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
5.5        From the details of inspections carried out by MCI during the period 1995-96 to 1999-2000, the 
Committee finds that in majority of the colleges, deficiencies have been pointed out as indicated

prescribed for the   MBBS course.   The entire course has been divided into three  phases.   Phase I (two 
semesters) consists of pre-clinical subjects i.e. Human Anatomy,  Physiology including Bio-Physics, 
Bio-Chemistry and introduction to Community Medicine  including Humanities.   Phase II (3 semesters) 
consists of Para-clinical/clinical subjects.  Para-clinical subjects shall consist of Pathology, 
Pharmacology, Microbiology, Forensic Medicine including Toxicology and part of Community 
Medicine.   Phase III will be of 4 semesters.   The clinical subjects to be taught during Phase II and III 
are Medicine and its allied specialties, Surgery and its allied specialties, Obstetrics and Gynecology and 
Community Medicine.

curriculum which is being monitored by MCI through periodical inspections.

XII      TRAINING  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
12.4     Committee’s attention was also drawn to the fact that young doctors are not inclined to join 
teaching profession.   General  perception is that at the time of joining medical education, most of the 
students make up their mind to do private practice since it provides financial gain of varying nature to 
the practitioners in comparison to the doctors going for teaching profession.   However, it can also be 
said that teaching job actually serves as a good launching pad for private  practice after gaining

XV       PROBLEM OF SHORTAGE OF DOCTORS IN RURAL AREAS – REMEDIES 
THEREFOR  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
15.1     Acute shortage of doctors in rural areas is a problem being faced in the entire country.   No State 
can be said to be not facing this problem, only its acuteness can be varying in different states.   The 
Committee finds that the main reason for the paucity of doctors in rural areas is the lack or inadequacy 
of facilities available in PHCs/hospitals.   Nobody would deny the fact that almost all PHCs in the 
country are ill-equipped.  They lack necessary facilities for treating even minor ailments whereas ground 
reality is that generally very complicated cases are handled there.   Another de-motivating factor is the 
disparity in the living conditions in the rural areas vis-à-vis  urban areas.  Geographical location is not 
convenient, and  even basic amenities like  proper roads, electricity and water, education for children, 
entertainment etc. are not there.  The situation gets more aggravated because doctors who man the PHCs 
are generally young pass-outs possessing only theoretical knowledge, practical exposure of ground 
realities virtually being nil. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
15.2     A number of suggestions were made for strengthening the rural services.   One suggestion made 
was that there can be two types of doctors  - one for rural areas and the other for urban areas.   Services 
of diploma doctors (three years course) can be utilized in rural areas.  However, the Committee is not 
inclined to agree with this view mainly because equal standards are required to be maintained for both 
rural and urban areas.   One must not forget the fact that rural masses although generally illiterate are 
gradually realizing the harm caused by unregistered doctors  practising in rural areas.   The Committee 
strongly feels that creation of a class within a class will not be appropriate.  Such a distinction would be 
detrimental to the entire medical profession. 
ACTION TAKEN 
The Three-years Licentiate Medical course has been discontinued since long and the MCI has expressed 
its reservation about is revival. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
15.5     The Committee would also like to emphasise that during internship period, PHC posting should 
be strictly adhered to and monitored as it would motivate them towards rural service later on.  The 
Committee also feels that  there should be an orientation programme before doctors posted in rural areas 
join their duties. 
ACTION TAKEN 
15.5     The recommendation of the Committee will be considered by the Council alongwith the on-
going review of the Graduate Medical Education Regulation 1997 being undertaken by the Council.  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
            While the Committee considers it necessary that doctors must serve rural areas.  There 
cannot be two opinions about it.  However, with regard to the duration of the period the 
Committee has  a flexible approach.  In view of the long  gestation period in these cases, the 
Committee feels that an effective system with lesser duration of even six months should suffice.  
Doctors should be given the choice to adopt a village nearest to their place of residence or work.  
They should be required to maintain a record of their visits, which should be at least 3 days a 
week, and the name and address of patients attended with the nature of disease and the diagnosis.  
The record of visit should as far as possible, be signed by any member/functionary of the 
Panchayat but this should not be compulsory.

XVI     BRAIN DRAIN 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
16.1     The Committee observes that the problem of brain drain is being faced at two fronts – one being 
from one institution to another inside the country and the other being flight of young talent to foreign 
institutions.   The Committee has been given to understand that this malady has penetrated even premier 
medical institutions.   On the one side,  national level institutions like PGI, AIIMS are facing shortage of 
faculty strength due to faculty members joining foreign institutions primarily for job satisfaction.   The 
other cause of serious concern is the silent brain drain in the form of voluntary retirement or taking  up 
regular jobs by Govt. medical  college teachers in private medical colleges.   Better working conditions, 
monetary benefits and more opportunity for undertaking research activities can  be  cited as the main 
factors responsible for this phenomenon.   The Committee observes that there is another aspect of this 
problem.   Young pass-outs do not get to know all the opportunities  which are available in the country.   
There is a need for evolving a facility  on the pattern of Recruitment agencies coming to the campuses of 
premier technical institutions for placements.   The Committee is of the firm view that  remedial steps 
need to be taken for creating best job opportunities  thereby retaining our young talent in the country.  
The Committee also feels that if necessary, students may be asked to pay back in easy instalments, 
wherever Government  funding is there.    Modalities in this regarding may be explored. 
ACTION TAKEN 
16.1     At present, in terms of Emigration Act the doctors and nurses fall under the exempted category 
of 'Emigration Check Not Required'. However, the MCI is of the view in the last 10-15 years the exodus 
of doctors has come down considerably due to the expansion in the medical and health facilities in the 
country.  Some of the foreign countries have also imposed stringent conditions on recruitment of doctors 
from abroad which has further curtailed the problem of brain drain.  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE: 
            The Committee does not quite agree that exemption of `ECMR’ under the Emigration Act 
is a reason for the problem of brain-drain.   The Committee would like this to be substantiated 
with facts and figures that during the last 10-15 years, the exodus of doctors has come down 
considerably due to expansion in the medical and health facilities in this Country.   The 
Committee feels that brain drain is a serious malady and that in medical profession where lot of 
tax payers money is spent on the education and training of medical students.  Tackling this 
problem may be difficult but not impossible.  What is needed is to adopt a carrot and stick policy 
in curbing this malady; purely punitive measures would not do.  Department should with the help 
of Department of Science & Technology work out a multi pronged strategy for curbing the brain 
drain in a time bound manner. 
XVII    MUSHROOMING OF LABS/DIAGNOSTIC CENTRES 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
17.1     Diagnosis of diseases based on clinical impressions alone can have fallacies even in experienced

indirectly led to a  mushroom growth of Labs/Diagnostic Centres  conducting CT Scan and MRI and 
other sophisticated tests all over the country.   The Committee has been given to understand that such 
centres are not generally manned by qualified medical    personnel.   The doctors treat their patients on 
the basis of reports given by such centres which sometimes give out incorrect interpretation of patient’s

comprehensive legislation to check  the mushroom growth of  such centres.

III        MEDICAL COUNCIL OF INDIA (MCI) 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.1       Medical Council of India (MCI) is a statutory body which was established under the  Indian 
Medical Council Act, 1956.   It is a nodal body assigned the task of processing the proposals for 
establishment of a new medical college, starting  of a new or higher course of study or training and 
increasing of admission capacity in any course of study  or training.      Other major function  of MCI is 
regulating the standard of medical education by carrying out regular inspections of different medical 
colleges  located all over the country in accordance with the  provisions of the Act and Regulations 
made thereunder. The Council is also empowered to recommend withdrawal of recognition in respect of 
any college based on its inspections.   Thus, it can be said  that MCI acts as the watchdog  for 
maintaining  the standard of medical education in the country. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.2       MCI is composed of both elected and nominated members.   As laid down in Section 3(1) of the 
IMC Act, 1956 under the elected category, one member of the medical faculty from each university, one 
member from each State in which a State Medical  Register is maintained and seven members to be 
elected  from amongst themselves by persons enrolled on any of the State Medical Registers are 
included.   Under the nominated category, one member from each state is nominated by the Central 
Govt. in  consultation with the State Govt.  and eight members are to be nominated by the  Central 
Govt.   Thus,  composition of MCI was envisaged to be well represented having members from all the 
required  categories. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.3       The Committee has been informed that  as on 21st June, 2001, the  total membership of MCI is 
113 out of which 77 are filled  up and 36 are vacant.   Out of 77 members in position, 34 belong to the 
nominated category and 43 are from the elected category.    Out of the total number of 36 vacancies, 35 
are from the  elected category.   The Committee observes that the  present composition of  MCI cannot 
be said  to be of an All India  character.   This is all the more evident as only  fifteen members form the 
quorum  of the Council and all the acts of the Council are   decided by a majority of the members 
present and voting. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.4       The Committee notes that out of 36 vacancies in the  113-member Council, 21 are in the seats 
Page 25 of 36133rdReportofHRd
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report133rd.htm

reserved for Universities.  Reason for vacancies in this category, as intimated by    the Department is 
non-constitution/non-reconstitution  of Senate or Court of the Universities or  meetings of the 
Senate/Court not being held for a long time.    What is a cause of  serious concern  is that Universities 
are simply not responding to the reminders  sent by the Council and the Central Govt. from time to time 
and vacancies are continuing in some cases for the last 10-15 years. 
3.5       In some states, a number of Universities now fall under the jurisdiction of Health Universities  
established in the recent years.   This development has led to a peculiar situation.   By virtue of coming 
under the jurisdiction of a Health University, such Universities   have lost their right of being 
represented in the Council.   On the other hand, Health Universities  cannot send their nominee to the  
Council as they do not have any Senate.   Thus, as many as 21 Universities over and above 56 eligible 
Universities are not represented in the Council.   Health Universities   having a  large number of medical 
colleges under their  jurisdiction, specially  in southern  and western states have no say in the decision-
making apex body on medical education. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.6       Out of 15 seats representing the Registered Medical Graduates (RMG) Constituency, 7 are lying 
vacant for varying periods of time.   The Committee has been informed that the  main reason for 
vacancies   in this category is that Returning Officers who are quite often the Registrar, State Medical 
Council or the State Director of Medical Education, keep on changing due to change of incumbents  and 
in some cases voters’ list has not been prepared up-to-date.   The Committee is constrained to observe 
that in spite of funds towards expenses for conducting the  election being provided by the Council, the 
Returning Officers  are simply not responding to the reminders of the  Council. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.7       Situation is equally disturbing so far as seats representing Licentiate Group are concerned.   At 
present, all the seats are lying vacant.   The Committee  has been given to understand that Asstt. Director 
General, Directorate General of Health Services was appointed as the Returning Officer on 21st 
January,1997.   However, as late as on 12th June, 2000, the Assistant Director-General approached the 
Central Govt. with a   request to be spared from the responsibilities of Returning Officer due to his 
transfer to Lady Hardinge Medical College.  Thereafter,  ADG of Health Services was appointed as the 
Returning Officer w.e.f. 19th June, 2000.   It  has been informed that he has so far received lists of 
registered licentiates from 12 State Medical Councils and the remaining 6 State  Medical Councils have 
also been reminded.  The Committee feels that chances of election process being completed in the near 
future seem to be very dim. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.8       The Committee is of the strong opinion that procedure for election of different categories of  
posts to the Council is too rigid.   There is an urgent need for streamlining  the election procedure, more 
so, if the representative composition of the Council as envisaged in the IMC Act, 1956 is sought to be 
maintained.   The Committee has been given to understand that a proposal of the Council for bringing 
out amendment in the relevant provisions of the Indian Medical Council Rules, 1957 for expediting 
election of members from Medical Faculty of Universities is pending with the Central Govt.  since 15th 
February, 1999.    The Committee recommends that the Central Govt. should take immediate steps in the 
matter.   The Committee would also urge upon the Central Govt. to take up the issue of non-completion 
of election process for other categories of seats with the concerned State Govts and impress upon them  
to expedite the same.   The Committee recommends that the Central Govt. should review the various 
provisions for constituting the Council laid down in the Act and the Regulations made thereunder for 
removing the anomalies therein. 
ACTION TAKEN 
3.1to3.8           The Central Govt. has already initiated action to amend the IMC Act 1956 to ensure that 
the vacancies in the Council do not remain unfilled for long and that the Council remains fully 
represented.  After this new law has been enacted, appropriate amendments in the Election Rules for 
various categories of members will be undertaken.

RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
4.1       Section 10A of the IMC Act, 1956 deals with the procedure for obtaining permission for 
establishment of a new medical college, starting a new or higher course of study or training and  
increasing the admission capacity. There also exist Minimum Standard Requirements for a Medical

4.2       By and large, the feedback which the Committee received with regard to the procedure and 
various norms/conditions prescribed for opening a new medical college, starting a new course and

growth of medical colleges.  However, it was pointed  out time and again that these norms need to be 
implemented stringently and objectively.   Besides that, some reservations were also voiced about the 
practicability of some of the norms, like requirement of minimum land specially for hilly, tribal and 
metropolitan  areas, very high amount of bank guarantee, requirement of infrastructure in the medical

XVIII  INDIAN MEDICAL SERVICE  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
18.1     The Committee observes that  teachers of Govt. medical colleges are governed by varying 
service conditions, by and large, dependent on the financial health of the Institution.  As a result, 
although MCI Regulations specifically provide for Full-time medical teachers, there are different 
categories  of medical teachers – Full-time, Honorary, teachers on contract, teachers entitled to private 
practice.   Salary  and other incentives payable to a  Govt. medical  teacher also vary from state to state.  
There are states where inter-change between teaching and non-teaching cadre is permissible,  other 
states are there where  district identity of teaching cadre is being maintained.   Besides that, Govt. 
medical college teachers  are also liable  to be transferred within the state.   Another problem pointed out 
is that these teachers are   under dual control – State Health Department and Directorate of  Medical 
Education. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
18.2     During the course of its deliberations, the issue for having an Indian Medical Service on the lines 
of IAS/IPS was raised.   The Committee observes that although it is a welcome idea, there are some 
inherent problems which may arise later on.   First is the difference between  the nature of jobs.   
Medical Service is mostly research-oriented, teaching job whereas IAS/IPS   is administration based 
service.   Secondly, it may not be  feasible as regional interest are not likely to be served.   The 
Committee  would also like to point out that there were strong reservations about  transfer policy being 
followed in the States.   Feedback which  the Committee received during its study-visits was that 
teachers, by and large were not in favour of being transferred even within a  State.   Not only this,  
Health being a State subject, it will be very difficult to create such a cadre and its implementation would, 
therefore, be difficult for obvious reasons.   The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that this issue 
needs to be subjected to wide-scale discussions in the medical fraternity before taking any decision. 
ACTION TAKEN 
18.1&18.2       The suggestions of the Committee for placing the proposal for creation of Indian Medical 
Service for discussion among the medical fraternity will be taken into account for initiating such a 
discussion. 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE 
  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee is  aware of the provision of Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, which lays down 
that any University having a medical faculty is entitled to send one member to the Council.   
However, the problem is that some Universities are still un-represented  in the Medical Council as 
they do not have a Senate in existence.   In view of this, the Committee recommends that sincere 
efforts be made for the constitution of Senate in such Universities so as to enable them to be  
represented in the Indian Medical Council.(Para No.3.5)  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee notes that the Medical Council of India has proposed  appropriate  amendments 
in the Act for the purpose  of strengthening the Council with more regulatory authority. The 
Page 30 of 36133rdReportofHRd
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report133rd.htm

Committee, however, feels that empowering the Council alone will not remedy the situation, as 
monitoring of the standards of Medical Education by State-run Medical colleges/universities has 
to be done from close quarters.   The Committee, reiterates its recommendation that despite the  
administrative and financial constraints, the possibility of setting up four regional councils in 
Southern, Northern, Eastern and Western parts of the country should be explored simultaneously 
by both the Central Government and the Medical Council of India.  The Department should take 
up the establishment of State Medical Councils in the States where they are not presently existing, 
besides reviewing their role. (Para No.3.11)   
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
            The Committee is of the view that the Department appears to have tried to evade any reply 
to the particular case of B.R.D. Medical College, Gorakhpur, U.P. which is the most glaring 
example of the tardy application of MCI regulations.  The Committee, therefore,  reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that a time-bound and result oriented inspection procedure is required to 
be  laid down if standard of medical education is to be maintained.  The Committee would also 
like the Department to respond to its observation that rates of different categories of inspections 
need to be reviewed and made reasonable as they are too high. (Para No.5.4 to 5.6) 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
            Despite the recommendations made by the Committee from time to time in this regard, 
constraints of the government including that of the State Governments and with due regard to the 
judgments given by the apex court from time to time, the Committee feels that the process 
regarding admission needs to be made as fair as possible.  The role of money, whether it is in the 
form of the capitation fee or under the table or in any other form must come to an end.  It has to 
be recognized that the influence of money here has a chair reaction thereby affecting the poorest 
of the poor and the middle class of the society who cannot bear the costly treatment in posh 
private hospitals whether it is a case of minor treatment, surgery or for that matter the major 
surgery.  These hospitals, clinics etc. have become shops where the first question that is asked to a 
patient whether the expenditure on his treatment is going to be reimbursed so that they can use 
their razor on the pocket of the patient accordingly. (Para No.7.4) 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE: 
The Committee in its 112th Report noted that no time-frame had been specified for updating the  
curriculum and that the review of the Graduate Medical Education Regulations could not be  
completed even after the lapse of a period of  twelve months since this report was presented.   The 
Committee views  this lackadaisical approach of  the Department seriously and    observes that not 
only the said review be expedited but the fixed curriculum should also be updated at regular 
intervals. (Para No.10.1to 10.4) 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee has been informed that  the curriculum for MBBS,  as prescribed in the Graduate 
Medical Regulations, 1997,  is mandatory for all concerned to follow. However, it was brought to 
the notice of the Committee that these regulations were not being followed by all the Universities, 
resulting in variation in the standards of medical education being imparted in different medical 
colleges. The Committee feels existence of rules in the Rules book is one thing and having no rule 
is better  than having one  and not being able to ensure its adherence. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that a permanent mechanism  should be evolved to ensure 
strict adherence of  said regulations by all the concerned universities. (Para No.10.5) 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
            The Committee notes with satisfaction that the MCI agrees with its observation about the heavy 
curriculum at under graduate level as well as need for optimizing it.  The Department, however, has not 
indicated its plan or intention of undertaking their exercise which it ought to have done in its reply.  The 
Committee would like to know steps taken/proposed in this  regard. (Para No.10.6 to 10.8) 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE: 
            The Committee would like to refer to the reply of the Department to Para 12.4 of the ATN

wherein the  Department,  in response to the recommendation of the Committee to attract bright 
students towards teaching, replied that in the absence of an organisation like UGC for providing 
financial assistance in the field of medical education, there can be no Central initiative for 
attracting the bright students towards teaching profession. 
            The Committee would like to mention that the proposal for having a  Central agency on 
the  pattern of UGC and AICTE was initially discussed in a meeting taken by the Member, 
Planning Commission and the broad guidelines for establishing  such a Commission  were also  
worked out.   However,  subsequently in 1997, with the approval of the then Health Minister  it 
was decided to keep the proposal in abeyance. The Committee further notes that the Draft 
National Health Policy 2001, envisages the setting up of Medical Grants Commission for funding 
new Govt. medical colleges and upgrading the existing Govt. medical colleges   The Committee is, 
therefore, not inclined  to accept that the Medical Grants Commission cannot be established due 
to scarcity of funds and strongly recommends that the Department should take all necessary 
measures for the establishment of Medical Grants Commission. (Para No.11.9)    
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE: 
The Committee feels that the steps taken by the Department to deal with the acute shortage of 
teachers in  non-clinical and Para clinical subjects would not serve the desired purpose unless, the 
teaching profession as a whole was made attractive.   Moreover, there is, in general, an acute 
shortage of teachers in almost all subjects.   The Committee, therefore,  feels that the Department 
should endeavour to find a permanent solution for this problem. (Para No.12.4)   
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
            While the Committee consider if necessary that doctors must serve rural areas.  There 
cannot be two opinions about it.  However, with regard to the duration of the period the 
Committee has  a flexible approach.  In view of the long  gestation period in this cases, the 
Committee feels that an effective system with lesser duration of even six months should suffice.  
Doctors should be given the choice to adopt a village nearest to their place of residence or work.  
They should be required to maintain a record of their visits, which should be at least 3 days’ a 
weak, and the name and address of patients attended with the nature of disease and the diagnosis.  
The record of visit should as far as possible, be signed by any member/functionary of the 
Panchayat but this should not be compulsory. (Para No.15.5) 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE: 
            The Committee does not quite agree that exemption of `ECMR’ under the Emigration Act 
is a reason for the problem of brain-drain.   The Committee would like this to be substantiated 
with facts and figures that during the last 10-15 years, the exodus of doctors has come down 
considerably due to expansion in the medical and health facilities in this Country.   The 
Committee feels that brain drain is a serious malady and that in medical profession where lot of 
tax payers money is spent on the education and training of medical students.  Tackling this 
problem may be difficult but not impossible.  What is needed is to adopt a carrot and stick policy 
in curbing this malady; purely punitive measures would not do.  Department should with the help 
of Department of Science & Technology work out a multi pronged strategy for curbing the brain 
drain in a time bound manner. (Para No.16.1) 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE: 
The Committee expresses its displeasure that comments/views on the draft Clinical Establishment 
Regulation Bill, which was circulated to the State Govts. and other agencies in February, 2001, 
have still not been received and desires that the matter may be finalized without further delay. 
(Para No.17.2) 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
            The Department has not responded to the Committees recommendation that government 
institutions generating income should be allowed to retain such income in the maintenance and 
upgradation of their institutions.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation in this 
regard and expects that Department to respond to it at the earliest. (Para No.21.5)

PLANNED DEVELOPMENT – ROLE OF AICTE 
Observation/Recommendation  
2.4  The Committee is of the view that the Department and AICTE should make all conceivable efforts 
for encouraging both Govt. and private initiatives in setting up technical institutions in N-E region. 
Action Taken  
Setting up of institutes on self-financing basis by Trusts/Societies is being encouraged.  As of now, 
there are 26 polytechnics, 8 Engg colleges, 7 Management Colleges and 18 PG programmes in the 
North Eastern Region. During 2001-2002, out of 3 applications received for setting up of Diploma 
Level, 2 were approved; 1 application received for degree could not be approved as it did not meet 
norms and standards. Also, during 2001-2002, 3 PG programmes were considered and approved. 
Observation/Recommendation  
2.11     It has been further informed that in April, 2000, AICTE had written to each State Government to 
prepare a perspective plan for developing technical education in the state and for qualitative 
improvement of technical education.    However, none of the States has given any perspective plan for 
development of technical education and the Council has so far not been provided with any feedback 
from the State Govts. regarding the quality of technical education, manpower requirement, employment 
opportunities etc.   The Committee is of the view that AICTE should impress upon the State Govts. to 
furnish the required information at the earliest.  
Action Taken  
Noted for compliance. 
INCONSISTENCIES IN DIFFERENT PROCEDURES AND NORMS – REMEDIAL SUGGESTIONS 
THEREFOR 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.2       The Committee was informed that in spite of academic eligibility prescribed by AICTE for 
Degree and Diploma  level courses, different States follow different academic eligibility criteria 
and there is no uniformity in the minimum cut off percentage which creates confusion.  During  its 
study visit to Chennai, the Sub-Committee was informed that in Tamil Nadu a minimum of 60% 
in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry individually and an aggregate of 70% at the 10+2 level is 
considered as entry criteria into the Professional courses.   However, in other States like 
Karnataka, Kerala,  Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and UT of Pondicherry, they require a pass 
percentage of  50 % .   Due to this differential eligibility criteria and other reasons, nearly 20,000 
seats  in Tamil Nadu remained unfilled this year.  The Committee strongly feels that there should 
be  uniformity at all India level for selection/eligibility criteria for admission in different technical 
education courses as far as possible.   The Committee, therefore, recommends  that the

registered with SCTE for the purpose of admission to Technical Institution for acquiring higher 
qualification as well as for the purpose of recruitment.  The practice which is followed by Medical 
Council of India (MCI), Council of Architecture and Pharmacy Council of India may be made 
applicable to the engineering graduates and Diploma holders. 
Action Taken 
Action may be taken only after discussion with the States.  The matter will be taken up in the National 
Consultation meeting. 
Observation/Recommendation 
3.11     The Sub-Committee, during its interaction with various experts, got an impression that AICTE 
has become highly centralised and there is need for decentralisation of its powers among its regional 
offices.  The Committee also feels that Regional Offices of AICTE  need to be strengthened by 
delegating more powers by the Head Office to avoid delay and for effective and smooth functioning of 
the Regional Offices.  However, it would like to point out that delegation of powers to the Regional 
Offices may be done only after sanction of permanent staff for the Council and its Regional Offices.  
The Committee would also like to point out that in view of tremendous increase in the number of 
technical institutions in the Country  in the recent years, required strength of staff should be sanctioned 
for Regional Offices.   
Action Taken 
AICTE has delegated the responsibility of approving Diploma Level Institutions to the concerned State 
Govts. On the basis of study by the Staff Inspection Unit (SIU), requirement of staff in Regional Offices 
will be determined. 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.12     The Sub-Committee  during its field visits after interacting with different functionaries gathered  
that the present norm of 5 acres land in metropolitan cities and 25 acres in rural areas for establishing an 
Engineering College does not seem to be practical.  In a Metropolitan City  like Mumbai it is very 
difficult to get the required land.  Even in rural areas, due to land ceiling, difficulties were being faced.  
It was suggested that the requirement of land at different places should be realistic.  In metropolitan 
cities,  where land is too scarce, vertical construction could be thought of which would require lesser 
land.    
Action Taken 
AICTE had constituted a EC Sub-Committee for review of norms and standards.  The report of this 
committee is now under consideration by the concerned All India Board’s (AIBs) and Regional 
Committees. The requirement of land in metropolitan cities is among  various issues considered by the 
Committee.  On submission of Report, the Ministry shall examine it for further necessary action.

Observation/Recommendation   
3.13     It was also pointed out that fixed deposit of Rs. 50 lakhs remains blocked which can neither be 
used by promoters nor by AICTE.  A suggestion was, accordingly, made that security deposit taken 
from institutions should be refunded in case  of those institutions which have shifted to their own 
buildings so that the amount could be utilised for further development of these institutions. Another 
suggestion made was that there should be option for either having a fixed deposit or bank guarantee.   
Action Taken  
            This aspect has also been considered by the EC Sub-Committee mentioned above. 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.16     The Committee notes that a Core Committee under the Chairmanship of the Special Secretary, 
Ministry of Human Resource Development has been set up for modification of norms and standards, 
including requirement of land and fixed deposit for technical institutions.  The Committee hopes that the 
Core Committee will finalise its Report at the earliest and take a realistic and practical approach in the 
matter. 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.19     In regard to the misuse of seats under NRI quota, the AICTE has stated that the provision 
of NRI seats has been long misinterpreted by  private institutions and universities.  The Council  
has now clarified vide its circular dated 3rd October, 2001 that unfilled seats under NRI quota 
shall automatically revert to payment seat category.   The AICTE has further clarified that it is 
the responsibility of the State Govts. to monitor admission and prevent the misuse of admission 
against NRI seats.   AICTE also clarified that besides the 5% NRI seats within the approved 
intake, AICTE has also allowed 15% supernumerary seats for Foreign National/Person of Indian 
Origin (PIO) through a separate notification dated March 31, 2001.   Seats remaining unfilled 
under the 15%  Foreign National/PIO quota shall not be allocated to anyone other than foreign 
students/PIO as per the said regulations.  The Committee hopes that the AICTE and State Govts. 
would take necessary steps to see that   NRI quota is not misused.    
STAFFING PATTERN IN AICTE 
Observation/Recommendation  
4.3       The Committee has been informed that AICTE has got its manpower requirement assessed 
by the Management Development Institute (MDI), Gurgaon which suggested that 60% of the staff 
of AICTE should be on permanent basis and 40 % could be on ad-hoc basis.   The Committee has 
been further informed that recommendations in the Report of MDI have been forwarded to the 
Department  for sanction of required posts on regular basis and the consent of the Department is 
awaited.  The Committee feels that ad-hocism in AICTE will not help in its effective functioning  
and, therefore it recommends that minimum regular posts may be sanctioned without delay.  
There should be balanced mix of regular and ad-hoc posts in AICTE. 
Action Taken 
Study of the manpower requirement of AICTE is scheduled to be undertaken by SIU.  Based on its 
recommendations, further necessary action will be taken. 
 INSTITUTION – INDUSTRY LINK

6.5       The Committee  would also like to point out that on a  larger perspective it is necessary to assess 
the manpower requirement of major industries and their needs.   Courses should be formulated 
accordingly.   Intake of students should be decided on the basis of requirement of industries.   In that 
way, unemployment and under-employment could be tackled  in a better manner or else industry would 
be requiring manpower as per their needs and we  would be producing manpower not fit for them.
