-           Devolution of financial and administ rative powers to State Lite racy Mission Authorities fo r
sanctioning of projects. 
-           The Scheme of Rural Functional Lite racy Projects is subsumed unde r the Scheme of Literacy 
Campaigns and Operation Restoration. . 
10.3     It is hoped that the revised mission would continue to consolidate the gains of previous years and
accelerate the growth of literacy movement. 
10.4     After experimenting with successive and alternative models of adult literacy, the NLM adopte d
the Total Literacy Campaign (TLC) approach as its pr incipal strategy for eradication of illiteracy. TLCs  
which provide basic literacy skills to the non-literate population pr imarily in the age group 15-35 years, 
have been launched in almost all the district s of the country. The TLC has certain positive
characteristics: area-specific, tim e-bound, participative,  delivery th rough voluntarism, cost-effective 
and outcome oriented. The campaigns are implemented through Zilla Saksharata Samitis as independent
and autonomous bodies, having due representation of all  sections of society. 
10.5     On conclusion of a TLC, Post Literacy Programme is there to enable the neo-literates to learn the 
application of literacy skill as problem solving tool, so that  learning becomes relevant to living.
Similarly, the Government of In dia had approved a new scheme of Conti nuing Education for Neo
literates in December, 1995.  Main thrust under it was given to setting up of continuing education centre 
which functions as a focal point for providing lear ning opportunities such as  library, reading room,
learning centre, training centre, info rmation centre, cultural  centre, sports centre etc. Besides that, the
Scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansth an or Institute of people's E ducation till now known as Shrami k
Vidyapeeth was launched as a multi-faceted adul t education programme ai med at improving the 
vocational skill and qualit y of life of workers and their fa mily members. Support was provided to
NGOs /VAs for carrying out activiti es such as running total and post literacy and continuing education
programmes, undertaking resource development activities through es tablishment of State Resource
Centres, organizing vocational an d technical education programme for neo literates, promoting
innovation, experimentation and act ion research, conducting evaluation and impact studies and
organising symposia and conference publication of  relevant books and pe riodicals and production o f
Mass media support aids. 
10.6     Out of 600 districts in the country, 587 have since been covere d under adult education
programmes; 174 under TLCs, 212 under post-Liter acy programme and 201 under the Continuing
Education Programme. About 96.69 mi llion persons have been ma de literate as on 31 March,2002.
About 60 percent of the benefici aries are women, while 22 percent and 12 percent belong to Scheduled
Castes and Scheduled Tribes respectively. 
10.7     The Committee, while appreciating the progress made towards literacy, also expresses its serious
concern over the functioning of various schemes of A dult Education.  At the end of Ninth Plan, NLM 
was expected to achieve around 70% literacy but as per census 2001, literacy rate is 65.38%.   The 
Committee notes with dismay the cut in allocation in the Ninth Plan ou tlay in priority schemes of adult
education viz., Literacy Campaigns  and Operation Restoration whic h have been reduced to Rs. 32.00
crore from 140.00 crore.  Even this allocation ha s been underutilized by 26 per cent. However, fo r 
Continuing Education for Neo-litera tes there was an increase in the allocation to Rs. 261.57 crore from 
Rs. 229.39 crore.  But, the funds under the  scheme remained unutilized to the extent of 11 per cent.  
The Committee takes these underutilization seriously and feels that these underutilization has come in
the way of  attainment of 70 per ce nt literacy by the end of Ninth Pl an.   The Committee hopes that the 
Department would make concerted efforts for optimum utilization of  allocated funds under the various
components/projects of Adult Education Programme.

Plan, NLM was expected to achieve around 70% literac y but as per census 2001, literac y rate is
65.38%.   The Committee notes with disma y the cut in allocation in the Ninth Plan outla y in
priority schemes of adult e ducation viz., Literac y Campai gns and Operation Restoration which
have been reduced to Rs. 32.00 crore from 140.00 crore.  Even this allocation has been 
underutilized by 26 per cent. However, for Contin uing Education for Neo-literates there was an 
increase in the allocation to Rs. 261.57 crore from Rs. 229.39 crore .  But, the funds under the  
scheme remained unutilized to the extent of 11 per cent .  The Committee takes these 
underutilization seriously and feels that these underu tilization has come in the way of  attainment 
of 70 per cent literacy by  the end of Ninth Plan.   The Co mmittee hopes that the Department 
would make concerted efforts for optimum utilization of allocated funds under the various
components/projects of Adult Education Programme. (Para 10.7) 
XI    GENERAL OBSERVATION 
               The Committee notes that the Bud get allocation for the current year has been kept
almost at the same  level as it was in the previous year. The Committee also takes note of the fact
that consequent to the amendment of the Co nstitution to provide for free and compulsor y
education to children in the a ge group of 6 to 14 years, it would be necessar y to create
infrastructure and implement the pro gramme which would, no doubt, require considerable
amount of funds. The Committee feels that this allocation would hardly be sufficient for sustaining
the ongoing activities of  the Department, particularl y the Universalisati on of Elementar y
Education, not to speak of startin g new activities b y the Department. The Committee , therefore,
recommends that the allocation of the Department needs to be increased suitably. (Para 11.1)       
            After considering the Demands fo r Grants of the Department  of      Elementary Education 
and Literacy and assessin g the pro gress of various pro grammes and pro jects administered b y it,
the Committee recommends that the Demands for  Grants of Rs.  4904.63 crore as sou ght by the 
Department of Elementary Education and Lite racy for the year 2003 -2004, under Demand No. 56 
may be approved. (Para 11.2)

PREFACE 
  
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Hundred thirty-ninth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand 
No.57) of the Department of Secondary and Higher Education, Ministry of Human Resource 
Development for the year 2003-2004. 
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the 
Department of Secondary and Higher Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development and also 
heard the Secretary and other Officials of that Department on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting 
held on 25th March, 2003. 
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on  
22nd April, 2003. 
  
  
REPORT 
I           INTRODUCTION 
Education is a nectar and has been considered a liberating force.    An educated society treads the path of 
rationality, breaks the shackles of ignorance and rigidity and takes the nation to a new high in the comity 
of nations. 
The system of education in India has broadly been divided in two categories: elementary education and 
secondary and higher education.  It has been observed over the years that new initiatives are being taken 
to strengthen school education. Programmes like National Open School (renamed National Institute of 
Open Schooling) are being strengthened to reach out more and more children in distant areas, National 
Council of Educational Research and Training is playing an active role in providing resource support in 
the areas of education research and training at school level.  The Navodaya Vidyalayas have been set up 
with the objective of providing a progressive and forward looking school system in the rural areas. 
Secondary Education  is of  crucial importance to our students  who spend formative years of their life 
here.    The secondary stage of Education   gains more importance as hardly 19% students reach the 
university level of education.   While changes have been made from time to time by the Government, 
fact remains that this stage of education does not lead students anywhere.   In fact, on the other hand, the 
subjects like English, Hindi and mathematics (i.e. modern mathematics) which has been introduced in 
the recent years etc.  are beyond one’s comprehension and on an average parents are not able to support 
their children financially.   These reasons alone have compelled students more so from the vulnerable 
sections of the society to drop out at secondary level only.    There is thus a need to involve the school 
more effectively to prevent drop-outs and reorient the education at this level, may be in the form of 
making it more vocational and need based so that in case of students who are not able to enter the 
university stage, at least the secondary education helps them to stand in the world on their own account. 
More so, vocationalisation of education is the need of the hour as the country faces a paradox of more 
and more number of children at entry level and corresponding flow of students at exit level of secondary

April 22 , 2003 
Vaisakha  2 , (Saka) 
  
ARJUN SINGH 
 Chairman, 
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on  Human Resource Development

and university stages with meagre opportunities in the development of one’s career, or, for that matter, 
employment.   
The Special Subject Group appointed by the Prime Minister's Office in its Report on Policy Framework 
for Reforms in Education of  April 2000 has estimated that as per the enrolment figures of 1997-98 two-
third of the eligible population  remains out of the school system and only 270 lakhs are attending 
schools at the secondary level.    
The challenge before the nation is how best to tap the potential of this upcoming workforce and 
gainfully employ them in projects of national importance and provide them a need based system of 
education and keep them away from the world of crime and ignorance and help them become a useful  
citizen of the society. 
II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 2.1        During the Tenth Plan, the approved outlay for Secondary & Higher Education is Rs. 13,825.00 
crore. The Planning Commission, while making the annual plan allocations for the year 2001-2002 had 
assured to give due priority to the Education Sector as soon as the funds were available through 
disinvestment. However, instead of additional funds being provided to the Department, the BE 
allocation was reduced at RE stage. Similarly, the projected outlay for 2002-2003 was Rs. 4223.37 
crore, whereas approved Plan allocation was only Rs. 2125.00 crores but this too came down  to Rs. 
1942.33 crore at RE stage. During 2003-2004 the Plan outlay (BE) has been fixed at the level of 
previous year's BE level i.e., at Rs. 2125.00 crore.  Non-Plan allocation for 2003-2004 is Rs. 2832.40 
crore.   
2.2       The Committee was informed that as state funding of the education sector has been inadequate 
and the desired six per cent of the national income could not be set apart for education, the Department 
has decided to constitute the `Bharat Shiksha Kosh' for mobilizing extra-budgetary resources by 
receiving donations/contributions/endowments from individuals and corporates, central and state 
Governments, NRIs and People of Indian Origin (PIO) in order to fill in the gap between actual 
requirement and the available budgetary support.     
2.3       In absence of any authoritative figures the Committee has taken the total outlay (plan and non 
plan) of Rs. 4749 crores and maximum number of students who registered themselves for 2002 
examinations i.e. 530401.    The  total outlay per head comes to Rs. 9345 half of which is non-plan 
expenditure.     The Plan  expenditure per student is thus Rs. 4500/- approximately which includes 
expenditure  on creation of infrastructure, peripheral  or administrative expenditure.   The net available 
per student is thus a pittance.    The Committee, therefore, observes that there is a need to provide more 
funds in this section as this is an investment to secure the future of our young generation.   Government 
must provide at least six percent of the national income to this sector which is much starved of funds.  
2.4     At the same time in many of the schemes/projects, the Committee, has observed  that substantial 
funds are lying with State Governments/NGOs and Utilization Certificates are not forthcoming from 
them for years together.  The Committee does not know whether these funds have been utilized at all.   
The Department must give a serious thought to this aspect and take necessary remedial measures for 
optimum utilisation of funds. 
SECONDARY EDUCATION 
III        NATIONAL COUNCIL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND TRAINING  
3.1       The National Council of Educational Research and Training  (NCERT) is an apex resource 
organisation to assist and advise the state Governments on matters related to school education.   It 
provides academic and technical support for qualitative improvement of school education.  Programmes 
and activities related to improvement of courses of studies, textual materials, support and ancillary 
materials for enrichment of instructions were undertaken to improve the content and process of 
secondary education and vocationalisation of education.  
3.2       The Committee notes with satisfaction that non-utilisation of funds has declined  from 22.68 per 
cent in 1999-2000 to about zero per cent by 2002-2003.   In fact, the NCERT has asked for more funds 
than Rs.15.05 crore which was allocated to it at RE stage for the financial year 2002-2003.   The 
Committee recommends that the requirement of extra funds by NCERT must be looked into with a view 
Page 4 of 19139thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report139th.htm

to help the organisation in its pursuits.              
3.3       The Committee notes that NCERT undertakes programmes and activities in relation to 
improvement of courses in vocational education. The developmental programmes/activities in progress 
include norms and standards for accreditation of institutions and programmes of vocational education, 
database for vocational education, software on question bank, competency-based curriculum on agro-
forestry, curriculum for NVQ in the area of transport  service, curriculum and modules in specific areas 
related to the entertainment industry, revision of general foundation course, modernisation of vocational 
curricula in purchasing and store keeping, accounting and auditing, pre-vocational instruction-cum-
practical manual on setting up of a plant clinic, instructional material for selected modules in marine 
fisheries, pre-vocational module in rural marketing, modular vocational course on e-business and course 
on small business management, module on dry cleaning, decorative candle making and instructional 
material for some vocational and pre-vocational courses.  
3.4       The Committee observes that there is need to cover more and more areas in a bid to vocationalise 
the education.   At the same time there is a need to introduce some ‘Earn and Learn’ kind of schemes to 
inculcate the feelings of self-sufficiency among the students.  
3.5       The Committee is of the view that there is a need to tap the vast potential of upcoming force of 
students who generally remain idle during holidays including summer vacation.  Millions of work days 
are just available at the asking with virtually no cost.   If they could be gainfully employed in projects of 
national importance or otherwise it will secure many purposes including out-station visits for students 
which are also a virtual education.   NCERT must give a serious thought to this aspect. 
IV   NATIONAL INSTITUTE OPEN SCHOOLING (NIOS) 
4.1       The National Institute Open Schooling (NIOS) has been pursuing its mission  of reaching the 
unreached by providing opportunities for continuing education to those who have missed opportunities 
to complete school education and developmental education through courses and programmes of general 
education, life enrichment and vocational education from primary to pre-degree level.  As an apex level 
resource organisation in school education through Distance and Open Learning Mode and as a National 
Board of School Education, the NIOS has been (i) developing curricula and self learning materials, (ii) 
organising Personal Contact Programme (PCP) at accredited study centres for enrolled students and (iii) 
examining them for its school level courses.   Steps are being taken to ensure that the NIOS curricula 
inter-alia take care of the children.    Keeping in view the educational needs of its clientele  groups, the 
NIOS has been providing flexibility in selecting academic,  pre-vocational and vocational courses as 
well as in examinations so that a candidate can learn and proceed according to his/her own pace. 
4.2       The Committee appreciates the efforts being made by NIOS in making  available  courses for 
physically, mentally and visually challenged children.   The Committee observes that NIOS must 
endeavour to reach more and more such children  and also try to make its system of education more 
responsive and need based.     
4.3       The Committee is also concerned about the recognition and acceptability of the Certificates and 
Diplomas for employment in both public and private sector.    While NIOS should endeavour to make its 
courses responsive and need based, Government must endeavour to ensure that the certificate and 
Diplomas awarded by NIOS are accepted  by the industry.  
V         KENDRIYA VIDYALAYA SANGATHAN 
5.1       KVS was set-up in 1965 as a registered body wholly financed by Government to establish, 
control and manage Kendriya Vidyalayas, the main objectives of which are to meet the educational 
needs of the children of transferable Central Government employees.  The Sangathan administers 843 
Kendriya Vidyalayas located in different parts of the country, out of which 706 Vidyalays are in the 
Defence/Civil Sector and the remaining are under the project sector.  
 5.2         The Committee has been informed that out of 706 Vidyalayas in Defence/Civil Sector, 612 
Vidyalayas are operating from permanent buildings and construction work is in progress in respect of 75 
Vidyalayas.  Besides that, there are still 68 Kendriya Vidyalas in respect of which land is yet to be 
transferred which are in Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, 
New Delhi, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, J&K, Jharkhand, Kerala, Maharashtra, Manipur, 
Page 5 of 19139thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report139th.htm

Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, UP, Uttranchal and 
W. Bengal.  
5.3       The Committee notes with concern the tardy pace of land transfers.   The Committee observes 
that certain transfer cases have been pending for last twenty seven years.     The Committee desires that 
these cases be looked into with a sense of urgency. 
5.4       The Committee has been informed that Government have since decided  not to open new KVs. 
While the rationale behind such a decision is not known to the Committee it feels that it is the 
responsibility of the State to cater to the  requirements of increasing population. Such a decision would 
be inconsistent with the requirements of the people.  The Committee also notes that the KVS intends to 
open some new schools without creating any additional liability on Non-Plan side.     
5.5       The Committee observes from the number of questions raised in the Parliament in the recent 
years that the level of discontentment among staff and teachers of KVS has been very high.   Rather, it 
appears that trade unionism  is  brewing in with the result each and every minute decision of the 
Government is questioned whether it relates to transfers, purchases, decision taken by individual 
authorities or Board.   Something   appears to be amiss somewhere.    The Department must check this 
tendency as the trade unionism  in education sector is not in the overall interest and more so in the case 
of students.   At the same time if a teacher is not contented and satisfied it would only affect the 
students.   The Department must evolve a ‘satisfaction platform’ where the grievances of teachers can be 
redressed. 
VI        NAVODAYA VIDYALAYA SAMITI 
6.1       Navodaya Vidyalaya is an  effort on the part of the Government in the right direction to spread 
the light of education through the length and breadth of the country. Navodaya Vidyalayas aim to 
provide good quality education to the talented children particularly from the rural areas.  At present, 
there are 468 sanctioned and 432 functional JNVs covering as many districts in 34 States/UTs.  During 
Tenth Plan, the Samiti proposes to acquire built up accommodation or construct permanent office 
buildings for its Headquarters Office, ten Regional Offices and 10 training centres.  The Samiti also 
proposes to expand sports activities, computer education programme, vocational courses etc. during 
Tenth Plan.  It is also proposed to start ten schools for gifted children. 
6.2       The Committee observes that out of 94 JNVs to be established during the Ninth Plan, only 80 
could be established.   The Committee feels that the remaining 14 JNVs should be established 
immediately.   As regards the number of students enrolled on 31.3.2002  there is still a gap of 11,191 
students to achieve the  target of 1,51,983 students fixed during the Ninth Plan.   The Committee has 
also been given to understand  that there have been considerable number of drop-outs and the 
Department intended to recoup the drop outs by enrolling more students in Class IX and XI in the 
functional Vidyalayas by the end of Ninth Five Year Plan. 
6.3       The Committee, feels concerned about students who have dropped out.   The Committee also 
notes with concern that the target of constructing 275 Vidyalayas buildings during the Ninth Plan could 
not be achieved.    The building constructed were less by 27 in number.    The Committee, recommends 
that the Department must examine the cases of drop outs as also the non-achievement  of the target of 
construction of buildings and take necessary remedial steps. 
VII      VOCATIONALISATION OF EDUCATION 
7.1     The Department has been implementing a centrally sponsored scheme of vocationalisation of 
secondary education at 10+2 level since 1988 and in its revised format since 1992-93.     The scheme has 
not been a runaway success and acknowledging this, the working group under the chairmanship of 
Director, NCERT, recommended for the establishment of block-level vocational training institutes, 
treating vocational stream at par with other streams of education, appointment of full-time teachers, 
coordination and utilisation of resources with other implementing agencies/departments/ministries, 
development of national vocational qualification of development of  a short-term course and linkages 
with major industrial outfits. 
7.2       The Committee appreciates the proposed changes.   In fact, the system of education developed 
durin
g British period and still being largely  followed aims at producing white collar jobs which are 
Page 6 of 19139thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report139th.htm

decreasing day by day because of Government's policy of down sizing and right sizing the 
Departments.    The students thus face a bleak future with growing unemployment.    The Committee 
observes there is thus a need to re-orient the system of education by making it more vocational to suit 
the present day situation and at the same time ensure balanced development as envisaged by Mahatma 
Gandhi.   Vocationalisation of the education should ensure that after completing certain level of 
education students can stand in the world on their own.   This would inculcate the sense of self 
sufficiency among students and possibly help in reduction of white collar crimes which are the result of 
one’s hunger and bleak future so far as employment opportunities are concerned.  
7.3       The Committee also desires that the participation of NGOs and voluntary organisations for 
implementation of specific innovative projects for conducting short-term courses should be encouraged 
more vigorously.    The Committee apprehends that grants given to many NGOs are not being utilized 
for the purpose for which these are given to them.   The Committee also apprehends whether the NGOs 
are pursuing the mission for which they have come up.   The Committee, therefore, feels the need for an 
effective monitoring system which can oversee the implementation of the schemes and note the concrete 
achievement, if any, made by the NGOs. 
7.4       The Committee also recommends creation of a data bank on employment and self employment 
status of the student who undergo vocationalisation courses in order to take stock of the contribution  of 
the programme. 
VIII      ACCESS WITH EQUITY 
8.1       This is a new Scheme taken up during Tenth Five Year Plan on the recommendations of the 
Working Group on Secondary Education for Tenth Five Year Plan. Under the Scheme the following 
components are proposed: 
1.         Strengthening of existing, programme of girl's hostels managed by NGOs.  
2.         One time assistance to reputed NGOs, Trusts, Societies and State Governments etc. for,        
setting up Secondary Schools.  
3.         Assist the Secondary and Senior Secondary Schools for opening second shift in  educationally 
backward districts.

second shift in selected schools. 
8.3          The Committee notes with satisfaction that the scheme would help in boosting girl's education, 
thereby, reducing the gender gap.  The scheme  would also help in the expansion of infrastructure.    
Much more needs to be done to create infrastructure to cater to the huge influx from elementary 
education level to secondary level.         
8.4        Against a financial target of Rs. 60.00 crore the expenditure incurred amounted to  Rs. 11.78 
crore which works out to only 19.63 per cent.    The utilisation of expenditure is thus far from 
satisfactory and indicates the performance at a snail’s pace.   
8.5       The Committee notes that barring Andhra Pradesh and, to some extent, Karnataka, the 
participation of NGOs in managing girl's Hostels has not been very encouraging.    The Committee 
would like the Department to analyse the reasons for this poor participation and take remedial  steps to 
ensure increasing participation of NGOs in this area.

X        UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION 
10.1     An amount of Rs.1630.55 crore has been proposed for UGC both under Plan and Non-Plan for 
the year 2003-2004. While the allocation under Non-Plan has been increased by Rs.13.80 crore as 
compared to the year 2002-2003, the allocation under Plan for 2003-04 in at the same level as  made 
during 2002-2003.  
10.2     Besides the role of giving grants to universities and colleges, UGC also advises Central and State 
Governments on the measures necessary for the development of higher education. It, thus, serves as a 
coordinating body between the Union and the State governments and the institutions of higher learning.   
10.3     In the reporting year 2002-03 (the first year of the Tenth Plan), the UGC had Plan budget 
estimates amounting to Rs. 516.75 crore for five sectors consisting of around 70 schemes/programmes. 
About 45 percent of the Ninth Plan schemes/ programmes have been dropped and 40 new schemes have 
been added for implementation during the Tenth Plan period. The five broad sectors of the Tenth Plan 
are general development of universities and colleges (219 crore Plan budget estimate), enhancing access 
and equity (29.50 crore), promotion of relevant education (70 crore), quality and excellence (99.25 
crore) and strengthening of research (99 crore). Out of the Plan budget estimate for the first year of the 
Tenth Plan, 10 percent of the allocation under each sector/scheme was to be allocated to North-Eastern 
universities and colleges. 
10.4     During the Tenth Plan period, the emphasis and focus would be on development of universities 
and colleges by making available infrastructural facilities, quality and excellence, access and equity with 
quality etc. During the reporting year, various UGC Visiting Committees were reviewing the 
implementation of various higher programmes during the Ninth Plan and assessing the financial 
requirements for the Tenth Plan period. The recommendation report of these Committees would be 
ready by the end of November 2002. Based on their recommendations Plan allocation would be made to 
the universities. 
10.5     It has been stated that the higher education system has seen a 13-fold increase in the number of 
universities and a 26-fold increase in the number of colleges since Independence. There are now 196 
universities, 76 Deemed Universities, five institutions established through state and central legislation, 
and 11 institutes of national importance established through Central legislation, and nearly 13,150 
colleges including around 1600 (12.7 percent) women colleges in the country in addition to the 
unrecognised institutions/foreign universities operating in the higher education sector. 
10.6     At the beginning of 2002-03, the total number of students enrolled in the formal system of 
education in universities and colleges has been 88.21lakh --- 11.66 lakh in university departments and 
76.55 lakh in the affiliated colleges. 
10.7     Eighty-four percent of the total enrolment was concentrated in the three faculties of Arts (46.13 
percent), Science (19.88 percent) and Commerce (17.87 percent) while the remaining 16 percent has 
been absorbed by the professional faculties.  Enrolment at the degree level has been 89 .13 percent 
(78.63lakh), at the Postgraduate level 9.25 percent  (8.16 lakh) and the remaining at the research and 
diploma/certificate levels. About 89.95 percent of all the undergraduate students and 66.02 percent of all 
the postgraduate students were enrolled in the affiliated colleges while remaining in university

departments. About 91.15 percent of the total research students were in the university departments. 
10.8       The enrolment of women students at the beginning of the academic year 2002-03 was 35.14 
lakh at all levels, constituting 39.84 percent of the total enrolment. Women's enrolment was the highest 
in Kerala (60 percent) and the lowest in Bihar (23 percent). About 88.25 percent of the total women

remaining 11.75 percent in professional faculties.  The women enrolment was the highest in the faculty 
of engineering and technology (3.75 percent) among various professional faculties. 
10.9     The number of doctoral degrees awarded by the universities (position as on January 2001) was 
11,450. Out of this, the Faculty of Arts had the highest number with 4,330 degrees, followed by the 
Faculty of Science with 3,737 degrees. These two faculties together accounted for 70.43 percent of the 
total number of doctoral degrees awarded. 
10.10   The strength of the teaching faculty in universities and colleges was 0.75 lakh and 3.52 lakh 
respectively, totalling 4.27 lakh in the beginning of the reporting year. Out of 0.75 lakh teachers in 
university departments, 20.22 percent are Professors, 31.53 percent are Readers/ Associate Professors, 
45.78 percent are Senior Lecturers/Lecturers and the rest are Tutors/Demonstrators etc. Out of 3.52 lakh 
in the affiliated colleges, 6.63 percent are Professors, 21.12 percent are Readers and their equivalent, 
66.70 percent are Lecturers and the rest are Teachers/Demonstrators/Teaching Assistants etc. 
10.11   It has been stated that the UGC, since inception, has been providing financial assistance for the 
development of universities and colleges, by making Plan budgetary provision under various 
programmes during different plans including the Ninth and the Tenth Plan. The financial assistance to 
Central and some Deemed Universities and colleges affiliated to Delhi and Banaras Hindu University 
was being provided both under non-Plan and Plan while assistance to state universities and their 
affiliated colleges was being provided only under Plan. During the Ninth Plan period (1997-2002), 
general development assistance to individual universities was based on the outlays determined.  Two-
thirds of the outlay provided was based on the Ninth Plan guidelines and one-third of the outlay was 
based on the performance of the individual university. The universities and colleges may utilize the 
development assistance being provided by the UGC for consolidation of existing infrastructure, for the 
modernisation of teaching, for research and administration and also for extension and outreach activities 
to meet the changing needs and challenges of higher education. 
10.12   Since the reporting year is the first year of the Tenth Plan, the modalities/guidelines for new 
schemes and the revised guidelines for the schemes/programmes of Ninth Plan (which are being 
continued in the Tenth Plan) were being prepared for implementation in universities and colleges. 
10.13   The Committee has been informed that out of 18 Central universities, 16 were being allocated 
development grants while 14 were being allocated maintenance grants in addition to development 
grants. During 2001-02, the UGC provided an amount of Rs. 598.69 crore to meet the maintenance 
expenditure of 14 universities and Rs. 81.31 crore as development assistance to 16 Central universities. 
10.14   Under the UGC Act, the state universities established after 17th June 1972 shall not be eligible to 
receive any grant from the Central Government, UGC or any other organisation receiving funds from the 
Government of India, unless the Commission satisfies itself as per the prescribed norms and procedures, 
that such a university is fit to receive grants. 
10.15   At present, there are 178 state universities. Out of these, the UGC has been making budgetary 
plan allocation for only 110 excluding medical and agricultural universities. However, the other state 
universities are also benefiting from the UGC under various other programmes (like special grants).  
Development grants including grants for specific schemes are provided to all eligible state universities in 
order to facilitate procurement, augmentation and upgradation of infrastructural facilities that were 
normally not available to universities from the state governments or other bodies supporting them. 
During the financial year 2001-02, Plan grants amounting to Rs. 175.62 crore were provided to 123 state 
universities for the purpose of development.  
10.16   The Committee appreciates the efforts of UGC in the field of university and higher education.     
Higher education system has made great strides under the aegis of UGC since independence as there has 
been a 13 fold increase in the number of universities and a 26 fold increase in the number of colleges.

Still the fact remains that only 19% of students are able to reach university education.    There is, thus, a 
need to make university and higher education system more need based and responsive to the 
requirement of students so that more students can avail of these opportunities.    
10.17   The Committee observes that UGC have developed a tendency to utilize the funds at the fag end 
of the year.    In the year 2001-2002, UGC could utilize only 72.84 % of its allocated plan funds till 13th 
March, 2002.   However, it reported  full utilisation of entire allocation made to it viz. Rs. 439.78 crore 
for the year 2001-2002 by 31st March, 2002.    The Committee feels that such a trend reveals poor 
planning and inadequate monitoring of the funds allocated to UGC.    The Committee feels that such last 
minute spending defeats the very objective of planned development.   The Committee therefore, 
observes that there should be adequate planning and monitoring to ensure the steady out flow of funds 
through out the year. 
10.18   The Committee is also of the view that UGC should encourage genuine   research activity and 
develop a mechanism for encouragement of only genuine research so that nation can make use of such 
research both commercially and academically.   In fact, R&D sector of our nation continues to be under 
developed.   The Committee feels concerned over this position and desires that it must change for the 
better.    The universities should have inter-disciplinary approach in its research activities which should 
commence from undergraduate stage. 
10.19  The Committee has been given to understand that there are a number of unaccredited universities 
in the country to which UGC does not appear to have given a thought. The UGC must initiate the 
exercise to determine the status of such universities and, if infrastructure available in these universities 
meets the standard requirements laid down in this regard, UGC must initiate steps to bring them to its 
fold.          
XI        NATIONAL COUNCIL OF RURAL INSTITUTES (NCRI) 
11.1     NCRI was set up by the Central Government in October, 1995 at Hyderabad to promote rural 
higher education on the lines of Mahatma Gandhi’s revolutionary ideas on education and to consolidate, 
network and develop institutions engaged in programmes of  Gandhian Basic Education and Nai Talim. 
11.2     The Committee has been informed that though NCRI was established in October 1995, yet it is 
in a formative stage. It has been functioning without a regular Chairman, a regular Member Secretary 
and without any regular staff.  The proposal for creation of post of a regular Chairman has been sent to 
the Cabinet Secretariat for seeking approval from the Cabinet.   A proposal is being processed in the 
Ministry of HRD for obtaining approval of Expenditure Finance Committee for the continuation of 
NCRI in l0th Plan. It, inter-alia, involves creation of 31 posts which are considered the barest minimum 
for undertaking activities of NCRI. 
11.3     The Committee views with concern the indifferent approach adopted to this episode and 
recommends that this be brought to the notice of the Minister and ensure that this unhappy state of 
affairs is brought to an end.  
XII       COMMUNITY POLYTECHNICS 
12.1     The polytechnic, as an institution, is well equipped with physical facilities (lecture rooms, 
workshop, hostels, equipments), which could be used for linking centres of knowledge and skills to rural 
communities. It has qualified and trained faculty, which could scientifically formulate, implement and 
monitor rural-oriented programmes and projects especially where transfer of technology is involved. It 
has large body of student population, which can be of tremendous help in making meaningful 
contributions to rural development given proper directions according to well-conceived plans. 
12.2     The MHRD provides one-time non-recurring grants-in-aid of Rs 7.25 lakh and annual recurring 
grants-in-aid to the maximum of Rs 7 lakh directly to selected AICTE-approved polytechnics whose 
proposals are recommended by the State Directorate of Technical Education.  As on date, there are 675 
community polytechnics in the country, out of which, 111 are running at the women's polytechnics. The 
region-wise distribution of community polytechnics is as under.

12.3     The community polytechnic is not different from a normal polytechnic. It is a wing of an existing 
polytechnic mandated to undertake rural/ community development activities through application of 
science and technology in its proximity, using infrastructure existing in polytechnics.  Activities under 
the scheme include: 
-           To ascertain the felt needs of the community through techno-economic job potential survey. 
-           To provide a platform for transfer of appropriate technologies to rural masses for the 
development on scientific lines. 
-           To provide technical/support services to the local community  
-           To train rural youth, women, SCs/STs, minorities, school dropouts and other disadvantaged 
groups of the community in need-based, non-formal courses/skills to enable them to obtain gainful 
employment (self/wage) 
-           To disseminate information and create awareness regarding development programmes for 
creating a problem-solving environment. 
12.4     Each community polytechnic serves through its five Village Extension Centres each covering 
10-12 villages of its proximity and the main centre is established in the premises of the polytechnic 
itself. Each community polytechnic provides training to about 600 rural youth every year. Thus, about 2 
lakh persons receive training every year. There is no age, qualification bar etc. for the trainees. The 
training courses are competency-based. The duration ranges from three to six months. 
12.5     The Scheme of Community Polytechnics has been reviewed twice at the national level. The first 
review was undertaken by the Kalbag Committee in 1987 and the second by the Luther Committee in 
1994. Both the reviews recommended the expansion of the scheme to cover all AICTE-approved 
polytechnics, besides suggesting a multi-skill competency-based training, a special programme for 
women, handicapped, street children and functional linkages with other rural development skills of the 
Central/ State Governments. 
12.6     Since the inception of the scheme to the end of Ninth Plan Period, about 12,00,000 persons have 
been trained in various job-oriented skills and about 52,000 villages have been covered under the 
scheme.   The most popular courses for female participants are as follows: 
(1) Garment making 
(2) Textile printing 
(3) Embroidery 
(4) Food processing 
(5) Secretarial works 
  
12.7     In order to enhance the job potential of the skills provided under the scheme, competency-based 
curriculum in about 135 trades has been prepared.  The testing and certification of level of skills 
acquired by the trainers has also been introduced under collaboration with local industries. 
12.8      The Committee appreciates the rural/community development activities undertaken by 
Community Polytechnics.     The Committee, appreciate the role of Community Polytechnic with a view 
to impart specialized skills to rural populace.    The Committee notes with concern that the number of 
community polytechnics in the eastern region is far less as compared to other regions.    Given the 
poverty and backwardness of the region, the Committee feels that there should be an increase in the 
number of such polytechnics there. 
12.9       The committee notes that  the plan allocation during 2002-2003 has been reduced to Rs.35.00 
crore at RE stage from Rs.63.00 crore at BE due to non submission of Utilisation Certificates by some 
of the Community Polytechnics and also because the revised funding pattern approval for the Tenth Plan 
period could not be obtained.

PREFACE
            I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this 
Hundred Fortieth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.58) of the Department of Women
and Child Development,  Ministry of Human Resource Development for the year 2003-2004.
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Women
and Child Development, Ministry of Human Resource Development and also heard the Secretary and other Officials of
that Department  on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held on 28
th March, 2003.
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 22nd  April, 2003.
 
NEW DELHI
April 22, 2002
Vaisakha 2, 1925 (Saka)
 
ARJUN SINGH
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Human Resource Development
 
REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
The Department of Women and Child Development was set up in 1985 as a part of the Ministry of Human Resource
Development to give the much-needed impetus to the holistic development of women and children.
The Department formulates plans, policies and programmes, moots proposals to enact and amend legislation affecting
women and children and guides and coordinates the efforts of both governmental and non-governmental organizations
working in the field of women and child development.   Apart from this, the Department implements certain innovative
programmes for women and children which are in the areas of training and capacity building, employment and income
generation, welfare and support services, awareness generation and gender sensitization. 
II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
            During the Tenth Five-Year Plan total    outlay for the Department is Rs. 13,780.00 crores.  Out of the total
allocation of Rs. 2653.91 crores for 2003-2004 Plan allocation for the year 2003-2004 is Rs. 2600.00 crores as against
Rs. 2200.00 crores and Rs. 2085.00 crores in BE and RE 2002-2003 respectively.  The non-plan allocation is Rs. 53.91
crores.
The Department has informed that the additional allocation of Rs. 400.00 crores in the financial year 2003-2004 is
proposed to be utilized for the following:
1.   To cover the expenditure on the ICDS programme assisted by World Bank which has been increased due to
enhancement in honorarium and restructuring of the ICDS III Project to include base cost, innovative and civil works
for 461 new ICDS blocks in four states and   provision for construction of model Anganwadi centres. Also, the project is
to be closed in September 2004 and it is expected that substantial residual liabilities   will be discharged in the financial
year 2003-2004.
2.  To meet the expenditure required for achieving the targeted expansion in number of operational projects in the ICDS
General scheme.
3.    To augment training of ICDS functionaries.
4.   To provide adequate funds under the Swashakti Project, which is scheduled for closure in May 2004 and the
performance of this Project is at peak.
5.  To give a major fillip to counselling services through upgradation and expansion of the scheme of Family
Counselling Centres at present being run by the Central Social Welfare Board.  
6.   To revise the norms for the scheme of Crèches and Day Care Centres to accommodate the escalation in cost of
provision of services due to inflation.
7.    To make provision of Rs 15 crores for Balika Samridhi Yojana against a nil provision in the BE 2002-03 as it was
understood in 2002-03 that the scheme was to be transferred to State Governments.  However, the decision of the

140thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report140th.htm[01-07-2016 16:17:55]
National Development Council is still awaited and hence this provision has been made in B.E. 2003-04.
The Department has further informed that the projected demand for the year 2003-2004 was Rs. 3240.32 crores but the
allocation has been made for only Rs 2600.00 crores against the projected demand. On this reduced allocation, the
Department has informed that the Ministry has taken up the matter for enhancing the allocation with Deputy Chairman,
Planning Commission and Finance Minister as well as with the Secretary, Expenditure and Secretary, Planning but the
allocation was not increased. Therefore, the allocation of funds has been made under various schemes as per the
curtailed budget.  The Department has informed that adequate funds have been earmarked for the following activities:
Time bound projects such as ICDS-World Bank, UDISHA and Swashakti, which are to be closed in 2004;
Special initiatives planned like expansion of family counselling services and upgradation of the norms of crèches and
day care centers;
 Sustaining efforts of Department for economic empowerment of women through   skill upgradation and training
schemes like STEP and Swawlamban; and
Strengthening support services for women in difficult circumstances under the Schemes Swadhar and Social Defence.
Further, the Department has stated that no scheme has been dropped/curtailed on account of the curtailed allocation.
However, against the   projected requirement of Rs. 1801.52 crores for ICDS-General in 2003-2004, the Department has
been able to provide only Rs. 1675.97 crores, which includes the provision of Rs. 231.65 crores for North-Eastern States
and Sikkim which may result in inadequate funds being available for targeted increase in operational blocks under this
scheme for the year 2003-2004. 
The Committee expresses its serious concern over reduction in allocation of funds for 2003-2004. It observes that the
Planning Commission should take a realistic view of the basic requirements of various Schemes before restricting the
allocation of funds from the projected Demands. The Committee recommends that the Department should make all
efforts to achieve the targets both physically as well financially and also utilize the existing allocation judiciously and
should not allow any scheme either being dropped or left neglected due to this curtailment in allocation.
At the same time the Committee feels that the women and children continue to feel neglected and insecure in the
society.  In fact, they are focus of all criminal activity that takes place.  Even otherwise there are many issues that
continue to be the cause of concern affecting women and children, be they within the four walls of homes, places of
work or schools or elsewhere, that need to be addressed.  The Department should, therefore, continue to review
periodically the effect of its programmes and Schemes on these sections of the society and modify them as per the
requirements of the situation with a view to ensure welfare and security of Women and Children.
During the year 2002-2003, the expenditure reported upto February 2003 is Rs. 1776.98 crores out of the allocation of
Rs. 2085.00 crores in RE.  Thus Rs. 308.02 crores remains to be utilized till the end of financial year. It seems the
situation of last moment spending was somewhat under control in 2001-2002, and it has again surfaced in 2002-2003,
with unspent balance of Rs. 308.02 crores.  It indicates that the Department has geared itself only at the fag end of the
Financial Year, which is not a happy situation, so far as achievement of the targets are concerned. The Committee had
observed noticed the trend of last minute spending, more or less, in each year of the Ninth Five-Year Plan and
commented upon this in  earlier reports.
             The Committee notes that the trend to utilize the funds in the last month of financial year is a regular feature and
observes that it is not a healthy trend and reflects adversely on the credibility of planning to utilize about 3% of the total
allocation in 15 days or a month before the close of the financial year despite the fact that the Committee recommended
in its earlier Reports that the Department should take corrective measures to avoid last moment spending so that the
funds could be judiciously utilized.
III        INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS)
            The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme aims at holistic development of children (0-6) and
pregnant & lactating mothers from disadvantaged sections.  It provides integrated services comprising:
supplementary nutrition,
immunization,
health check up,
referral services,
pre-school non-formal education,  and
nutrition & health education.
            The Department has informed that for the currently sanctioned 5652 projects the Scheme would continue in the
Tenth Five-Year Plan. Out of the sanctioned 5652 Projects, 922 are being funded with loan from the World Bank and
out of the remaining 4730 Projects under ICDS (General), 3873 were operational on 31
st March 2002.  The

140thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report140th.htm[01-07-2016 16:17:55]
operationalisation of the pending 857 Projects has been spread over the full Tenth Five-Year Plan period in view of the
constraints imposed due to limited allocation.  During 2002-2003, 152 pending projects were targeted for
operationalisation.
 
The details of these projects in some of the States are as follows
 
State               No. of  ICDS
Projects
   
     Sanctioned  Operational  
     2001    2002     2001    2002
Andhra Pradesh       363      363       251      251
Assam       196      196       107      151

Maharashtra       370      370       268      331

The Committee notes that there has not been any significant improvement in the number of Projects, which were
operationalised.  The states of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Uttaranchal have not shown any increase in the
number of operational projects even after gap of an year.  This shows the indifferent attitude of the State Governments
towards the operationalisation of the sanctioned projects.
            The Committee recommends that the Department must renew its efforts and approach the State Governments to
persuade them to operationalise these projects.
           
The National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) conducted an evaluation of the ICDS Programme in
entire India and submitted its report in 2001. The findings in the report indicate the following:
Around 62% of the women availed of Supplementary Nutrition.
60% availed of ante natal/post natal services
Around 56% availed of Nutrition and Health Education services 
42% availed of health check ups.
Percentage of mothers availing IFA tablets and health check up were reported to be about 40%.
Tetanus toxoid injections and referral services have received comparatively low response with 27% and 24% of women
availing them.
 
            The Committee notes with concern the findings of the Report which indicate that the maximum benefit of the
proposals made by the Department is almost out of reach of the targeted sections of population as it is evident from the
low rate of utilization of facilities by the beneficiaries. The Department should find out the reasons for the reluctance of
the people to avail of benefits of Schemes and take remedial steps accordingly.
 
Regarding high Infant Mortality Rate in the country particularly in some States, the Department has informed that
surveys bring out that IMR is significantly lower in ICDS areas compared to non-ICDS areas.  For example; in 1981-
1982 and 1992 the National IMR were 105 and 79 respectively whereas in the ICDS areas IMR stood significantly
lower at 88.8 and 71.3 in the respective years. (NIPCCD 1992) 
 
With the spread of ICDS to uncovered areas IMR is expected to decline further.  The Directory of Blocks of Ministry of
Rural Development indicates 5488 rural/tribal blocks in the country as on 31.3.1999.  Thus it would be seen that the
sanctioned rural and tribal blocks (5292) do not fully cover rural and tribal blocks.  Further, the Scheme covers only 360
urban slums.  With the growth of population over the years and rapid urbanization, there is a perceived need for more
Anganwadi Centres within the existing Projects, to cover the population as per the schematic norm of one Anganwadi
Centre for 1,000 population in rural/urban Projects and 700 population in tribal Projects and to increase outreach of
ICDS in urban areas.
 
The Committee recommends that there is an urgent need to sanction additional ICDS projects for the uncovered

140thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report140th.htm[01-07-2016 16:17:55]
blocks/urban slums.  In addition to this more anganwadi centres should be opened and feasibility for relocation of
existing centres should be explored.
 
IV        WORLD BANK ASSISTED ICDS PROJECT
 
            The Department has informed that the World Bank provides credit to Centrally sponsored projects.  In these
projects, civil works outdoor and indoor play equipment display boards, medicine boxes, IFA tablets and some quality
improvement activities are also provided over the above the items admissible in ICDS General Project.
 
At present one of such project namely; ICDS-III Project (1999-2004) is being implemented in the States of Kerala,
Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh.  The Committee notes that out of 318 new projects covered
under this scheme, 310 projects have already been operationalised and remaining 8 projects are likely to be
operationalised in few months.   The Committee has been informed that out of the 5652 Projects under ICDS, 922
projects in 10 states are being assisted by loan from the World Bank. Of these 735 were operational on 31
st March 2002,
and the operationalisation of the remaining 187 was expected to be achieved in 2002-2003.
 
            The allocation in BE 2003-2004 has been enhanced from RE 2002-2003 of Rs. 378.77 crores to Rs. 600.00
crores. The Department has stated that the enhanced allocation has been made for the following items:
 
(i) Restructuring Activities
 
Provision for Base-cost in 461 new ICDS blocks in the States of Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh & Jharkhand
together with new Adolescent Girls Scheme and Civil works in these States:
Provision for additional honoraria to (a) Anganwadi Workers/ Anganwadi Helpers in Madhya Pradesh, Bihar,
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand; (b) Kerala, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh:
Provision for construction of Model Anganwadi Centres:
 
(ii) Existing Activities
 
Provision for normal authorized activities under ICDS-III Project (including CPMU);
Provision for (a) normal authorized activities under ICDS-APER in Andhra Pradesh; (b) additional honoraria to
Anganwadi Workers/Anganwadi Helpers in Andhra Pradesh;
          During 2003-04, an allocation of Rs. 10.0251 crores has been approved for Management & Institutional
Development, which includes Project Management and on the same pattern there is an approved allocation of Rs. 5.00
crores for IEC.  The expenditure reported upto February 2003 is to the tune of Rs. 267.90 crores only out of the RE of
Rs. 378.77 crores.  The utilization of expenditure works out to 70% (approx.)
 
            The Committee takes a serious note of under utilization of resources placed at the disposal of the Department
and impresses upon the need for proper monitoring of the Schemes by both the Central and State Governments in future
and ensuring effective implementation.
 
V         ICDS TRAINING PROGRAMME – UDISHA PROJECT
 
            Project `UDISHA’ is a comprehensive training strategy for ICDS functionaries such as Anganwadi Workers,
Anganwadi Helpers, Supervisors, Assistant Child Development Project Officer and Child Development Project
Officers.  The Department has informed that after detailed 'discussions with all concerned, comprehensive guidelines,
for timely and qualitative implementation of the Project have been issued to States/UTs for formulating State Training
Action Plans for 2003-04 and 2004-05 (upto 30-9-2004) for
(i)         Fulfilling the physical targets for regular training as per the Project Implementation Plans,
Revision and adaptation of the training syllabi for ICDS functionaries,
(iii)       Qualitative and productive implementation of the 'Other Training', and 'IEC' etc.components; and
(iv)       All-round qualitative delivery.
 

140thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report140th.htm[01-07-2016 16:17:55]
            It was also decided that NIPCCD would not be undertaking any routine training programme.
 
The Department has further informed that States/UTs (except NE States) are in the process of identifying `State training
Institutes’ (STls) to undertake CDPOs/ ACDPOs etc training (hitherto being done by NIPCCD). These STls would also
provide guidance and directions to the Middle Level Training Centres. (MLTCs) and Anganwadi Training Centres
(AWTCs).  Further, the syllabi for job training and induction training of Anganwadi Workers has been revised to
address state-wise, contextual variations, States/UTs have also been given the option to incorporate 25% state-specific
component, if required.  As a part of restructuring of World Bank assisted ICDS-III Project revised allocation under
UDISHA are subject to 'Performance Based Review' i.e. better performing States would be given additional allocations
(if required by them) by curtailing the allocations of poor performing States.
 
The Committee welcomes the revision of syllabi for job training and revision of allocation subject to `Performance
Based Review’.  However, the Committee recommends that setting up of STIs should be expedited so that the training
programmes do not suffer a setback. The States should be given time frame to set up these Institutes and the Department
should constantly monitor the progress.
 
It has been informed that the budget provision for training programme was reduced from Rs 62.00 crores in BE for
2002-2003 to Rs 60 crores in RE of that year. However, in BE for 2003-2004 the allocation under this Head has been
made for an amount of Rs 76.50 crores. With regard to the targets achieved in imparting training under this project the,
details are as under:

VI        DAY CARE CENTRES
 
The Scheme of Crèches/Day Care Centres was started in 1975. It aims to provide day care services for the children (0-5
years) of casual, migrant, agricultural and construction labourers. The children of those women, who are sick or
incapacitated due to sickness or are suffering from communicable diseases, are also covered under the scheme. The
Scheme is designed to cater to low-income groups and, therefore, only those children whose parents' total monthly
income does not exceed Rs.1800/- per month are covered.  The Scheme is being implemented by the Central Social
Welfare Board through voluntary organisations and by two other National leve1 voluntary organisations namely, Indian
Council for Child Welfare and Bharatiya Adimjati Sevak Sangh' all over the country. The scheme covers 12,470 crèches
benefiting about 3.11 lakh beneficiaries.
 
Allocation for BE 2003-2004 is Rs. 18.00 crores whereas the BE and RE 2002-2003 were Rs. 12.00 crores and Rs. 8.00
crores respectively.  The actual expenditure upto Feb. 2003 is Rs. 6.75 crores.  The amount of unspent balance under the
scheme with CSWB for the year 2002-2003 as on 5
th March 2003 is Rs. 1.08 crores.  The Committee has been informed
that the budget provision in 2002-2003 was enhanced in view of the revision of schemes. However, the proposed
revision could not match availability of funds in the Tenth Five-Year Plan. Hence it was decided to restrict revision of
Schemes to upgradation of norms in line with increase in cost of delivery of services, which would be processed in

2003-2004.
 
The Committee observes that the Scheme at present caters to low-income groups in respect of which income does not
exceed Rs. 1800/- p.m. This aspect needs to be looked into whether the Scheme is in conformity with minimum wages
fixed under the law. Perhaps the minimum a construction labourer say a beldar gets is more than Rs. 100/- per day. In
these circumstances, it is doubtful whether the Scheme serves target income groups or whether the children from the
prescribed income groups are available.  Probably, this could also be the cause for low utilization of funds.
The Department has informed that it has initiated necessary action for introducing ISO approved standards for Crèches. 
Consultations have been held with BIS and Experts in this regard during 2002-2003 and a working group has been set
up for standardization of services based on experience gathered from running existing crèches and need assessment
service.
The Committee feels there is tremendous need to introduce ISO standards. At the same time, it is necessary to keep
these crèches free from all kinds of infection for which utmost cleanliness is necessary as children are more prone to
infection. The Committee, therefore, recommends that top priority be accorded for maintaining cleanliness.

The scheme earlier known as  "Training-cum-Production Centres", has been changed to " 'Swawlamban". It provides
training to women belonging to weaker sections in the traditional and non-traditional trades  than employing them on

canteen management, house-keeping has also been introduced. Norms for Call centre training were being finalized.

employed in various organisations and the employment, as far as possible,  should be on a regular basis.

like IT in rural areas. The Committee recommends that new programmes  may be added in Urban areas, but  traditional

XVI     SWADHAR
The  Scheme was launched in 2001-2002 in the Central Sector for the benefit of women in difficult circumstances.
Under the scheme, diverse projects were sanctioned for rehabilitation of widows in religious places,  Riot affected
women and children, victims of terrorist violence, mentally disturbed women  and victims of trafficking.  Besides this,
54 Helplines have been sanctioned for women in distress.
 
The Monitoring of the Scheme was being done at  three levels. Biannual Monitoring at District Level under the
chairmanship of District Magistrate, who would  submit his report to Secretary, Social Welfare/Women and Child
Development of the concerned State Government within 15 days. Secretary in-charge of Social Welfare, of the State in
consultation with other member of the committee shall meet at least once a year and monitor the project. At the Central
Level, Department of Women and Child Development shall also review the functioning of the Scheme.
           
The Committee has been informed that pension was being provided to very few `widows’.  There was a long waiting list
of aspirants.  Although the pension was granted by Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, the Committee
recommends that the Department should take up the matter with that Ministry and have this amount suitably enhanced
so that those in need could get the pension.
 
XVII    TRAFFICKING IN WOMEN AND CHILDREN
The Committee’s attention has been drawn to the problem of Trafficking in Women and Children which has
considerably increased in the recent years. The Committee recommends that preventive measures should be undertaken
in accordance with the following strategies:
Prevention of trafficking through the legal and criminal system, training of law enforcement officers,
Control and suppression of prostitution through  legal system,
Rescue and rehabilitation for women and girl victims of trafficking,
Protection for and awareness-raising among women and girls to prevent trafficking,
Enhance public awareness, particularly in relation to forced and child prostitution and other measures,
Awareness-raising among parents and guardians,
Provision of alternative employment and income-earning opportunities for women and girls, and
Through campaigns targeting parents on the long-term advantages of girls education.
XVIII   GENERAL
The Committee notes that every year new schemes are being added/ modified for the welfare of Children and Women.
However, the Committee recommends that instead of framing new schemes every year the Department should
concentrate on strengthening the existing ones with a view to enhance their utility and acceptability.

REPORT
I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       The main responsibility of the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports is to ensure qualitative and quantitative
improvements in Youth Programmes and also on broad basing and bringing about awareness of sports and physical
fitness amongst school children and youth.  Over the years, the Ministry has taken a number of new initiatives and
organized a large number of programmes in the field of youth developments and sports and physical education.   The
Programmes undertaken by the Department are mainly Sports and Games, Physical Education and Youth Programmes.
1.2       The Ministry pursues the twin objectives of man making and nation building i.e. developing the personality of
the youth as also involving them in various nation building activities.  To achieve these objectives, Ministry of Youth
Affairs and Sports has undertaken various youth welfare programmes which range from personality development to
vocational training, to promotion of adventure and entrepreneurial development.  Most of these programmes are
implemented by State Governments, autonomous organizations of the Ministry and non-governmental organizations. 
Financial assistance is provided to all the implementing agencies by this Ministry as per the stipulated norms.  The
major schemes for youth development are National Service Scheme, Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, National
Integration Programmes, Youth Hostels and National Service Volunteers Scheme, etc. and the same are financed by the
Ministry.
1.3       The Department also finances a number of programmes which aim at promotion of sports, including creation of
sports infrastructure in different parts of the country, grants for laying of synthetic surfaces, spotting and nurturing of
talents through the schemes of Sports Authority of India, grants to National Sports Federations, National
Championships, organisation of tournaments for rural youth, women in the North-Eastern Region.
1.4       In the recent past, the performance/standard of Indian Sports has definitely improved.  India’s performance in
2002 Commonwealth Games and Asian Games was commendable.  However, compared to International Standards and
pace of improvement in the International Standards, we have a long way to go.  The Ministry is making concerted
efforts to create infrastructure of a high standard in various parts of the country. 
            Since the promotion and development of sports is an ongoing process, Government of India, in consultation with
Sports Authority of India, Indian Olympic Association and National Sports Federations, is taking the following steps to
improve the standard of Indian sports:
Broadening the base-especially, for competitive sports;
Improvement in infrastructure;
Improving the knowledge of the Coaching Community;
Improving the practical knowledge of the Scientific Community to enable them to contribute along with the coaches to
enhance performance of sports persons;
Improved functioning and professionalisation in management of Sports Federations;
 Greater involvement of States in the development of Sports infrastructure and improved training of sportspersons;
Involvement of the private sector in adopting and sponsoring individual/specific sports disciplines; and
Creation of awareness in general public to have greater participation in sports activities.
Besides these, long term development plan prepared by NSFs also cover areas like athlete development, growth of
sports clubs, domestic and international tournaments, equipment and scientific support, management etc.
Youth constitute nearly 40% of India's population. It is, therefore, necessary not only to make this vibrant and strong
resource of the country beneficiaries of, but, also, valuable partners in the process of our planning and development. In
order that young men and women are able to contribute towards national development in a significant way, it is
important that they should be able to effectively participate in the process of decision-making. Towards this end, the
Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports has been constantly reviewing the policies and programmes concerning the Youth of
the country, so as to keep pace with the fast changing socio-economic scenario and also to address the emerging
concerns of the youth, a Draft Policy is stated to be in an advanced stage of finalization. A National Commission for
Youth has been set up to recommend to the Government measures to tackle effectively the problems faced by the youth
of India, with particular focus on youth unemployment. Two new schemes viz. Financial Assistance for the
Development and Empowerment of the Adolescents and Scheme for Establishment of National / State Youth Centres
are proposed to be implemented during the Tenth Plan.
