2.1       The Working Group for the Tenth Plan had recommended an outlay of Rs 3287.51 crores in respect of Plan
Budget However, an outlay of Rs. 2036.77 was agreed upon at the level of the Principal Adviser (Edn.) in the Planning
Commission in discussions with the Secretary (YA&S). Subsequently, the Planning Commission conveyed their
approval for an outlay of Rs. 1600.00 crore only. This was raised to Rs. 1625.00 crores to provide budgetary support to
the new scheme for the Adolescents, and was further raised to Rs.1825.00 crores, the additionally being provided,
exclusively, for the schemes relating to Sports Infrastructure.
2.2       Asked about the Projected demand of the Ministry it has been stated that for Non-Plan Budget a demand of
Rs.86.31 crores against which an allocation of Rs.55.30 crores has been approved by the Ministry of Finance. 
Regarding Plan expenditure it has been stated that the enhanced budgetary support of Rs.100.00 crores would be utilized
for various Schemes in the Youth and Sports sectors which were being broad-based, in terms of geographical coverage
as well as number of beneficiaries.
In the sports sector, higher allocations have been given to Sports Authority of India (SAI) for
strengthening/development of sports infrastructure, upgrading and procurement of technical equipment in SAI
regional/sub-Centres, upgradation of the facilities at Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium, and the expenditure on account of
the newly set up All India Council of Sports.
Other areas, where additionally budgetary support has been provided, included Grants to Sports Federations, scheme
relating to Infrastructure, the newly proposed scheme of Incentives for Promotion of Sports Activities, including Rural
Sports Programmes, scheme of Special Awards to Winners of International Sports Events and their Coaches.
Two New Schemes, namely, scheme for Dope Test, and scheme for State Sports Academies, were being launched
during 2003-04 for which allocations have been made.
In the Youth Sector, higher allocations have been made for the new scheme of financial assistance for the Development
and Empowerment of the Adolescents, which would be launched during 2003-04. Similarly, some allocation has been
made under the scheme of National Reconstruction Corps in anticipation of its continuation beyond 31
st March 2003,
subject to the outcome of an evaluation being carried out by the Planning Commission.
While the role and contribution of youth is of vital importance in all countries, it is particularly significant in a
country like India where the proportion of the youth in the country’s overall social and demographic profile is
continuously increasing. According to the 2001 Census, there were approximately 355 million people in the 15 to
35 age group, 74 per cent of whom lived in rural areas. The number was expected to rise to approximately 510
million by 2016. Both central and state governments need to harness the energies of this large group, providing
them with adequate infrastructure of world standards for excellence in sports at national and international
levels.
The Committee is constrained to observe that no organized effort appears to be forthcoming over a national scale to tap
the potential of the Youth. Youth are the foundation for the development of the country and unless emphasis is laid on
youth programme and put the youth on the right track and right direction, the ultimate goal of nation building can not be
achieved.  The Committee feels that in order to develop the youth, a yoga programme should be started throughout the
country for different age groups with a definite capsule of different sets of exercises provided for different age groups. It
should be as near to the homes of the people as possible. Adequate number of volunteers should be trained for the
purpose who may conduct the exercises in Yoga suited to different age groups. These exercises may be conducted in an
hour say between 5 to 6 a.m. throughout the country. It should be designated a national hour. The trained volunteers
may be paid an allowance for the purpose. This would infuse new energy & fitness among the people and help build a
strong nation. Further modalities, if any, could be worked out. The services of any existing organization could also be
utilized for the purpose.
III        THRUST IN THE NINTH FIVE YEAR PLAN
The thrust in the Ninth Plan was on harnessing Yuva Shakti (Youth power).  The National Youth Policy emphasis:
Involving young persons in various community-based nation building activities and a new scheme called National
Reconstruction Corps (NRC) to involve youth volunteers in such activities;

141thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report141th.htm[01-07-2016 16:19:47]
Youth empowerment and gender justice through an inter-sectoral approach;
Providing special attention to education, training and employment, health, environment, sports, recreation and leisure,
art and culture, science and technology, etc.; and
Developing the interest of youth in development-oriented programmes.
3.2       During the Ninth Plan, the NYKS was able to extend its activities to a larger number of villages and it now has
offices in almost 500 districts The NYKS took up several new initiatives to involve the rural youth - by motivating them
to organise themselves into youth clubs and self-help groups. Schemes like the NSVS, Financial Assistance to Youth
Clubs, Award to Outstanding Youth Clubs and Youth Development Centre have been successful in encouraging young
people to take up development-oriented programmes. The NYKS also took up major programmes under the
Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), being implemented in collaboration with Ministry of Rural
Development. The objective of the programme was to bring selected Below Poverty Line (BPL) youth above the
poverty line in three years. Watershed Management Programmes were also being implemented by the NYKS. In
addition, the NYKS also provided assistance to disabled persons for providing aids and appliances, running of 100 old
age day care centres, 30 Gandhi Millennium Youth Peace Centres, Wildlife Watch Centres, National Youth
Cooperatives and United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)-NYKS Youth Volunteers Against Poverty Awards
Programmes. The coverage under NSS increased to more than 1.7 million students.
IV        APPROACH TO THE TENTH FIVE YEAR PLAN
Government’s approach on Youth Affairs and Sports during the Tenth Plan period is reflected in the following paras of
the Approach Paper to the Tenth Five Year Plan:
            “Adolescent youth in the 10-19 years age group numbered 230 million, accounting for 22 8 per cent of the
population. It is proposed to target this segment of the youth population through specific intervention strategies that will
focus on youth and power, gender justice, youth health and responsible living.
            The major thrust will be on involving the youth in the process of national planning and development and making
them the focal point of development strategy by providing proper educational and training opportunities, access to
information on employment opportunities including entrepreneurial guidance and financial credit, proper platforms for
developing qualities of leadership, tolerance and open mindedness, patriotism, etc. 
The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports will play a pro-active and catalytic role in exploring and identifying
employment opportunities for the youth in coordination with other Ministries and Departments so as to optimally utilize
the investments in various youth-related schemes The Ministry will also play an active advocacy role in promoting
gender justice by sensitising the youth towards gender issues.
            Youth activities will focus on providing quality health services and will ensure that the youth have access to
information relating to reproduction, health issues, managing alcoholism, drug addiction, etc. 
            Value-based education will be imparted which will focus on respect for elders, tolerance for others' beliefs and
religions, compassion towards the poor and needy. The youth will be involved in the protection and preservation of
nature. Steps will be taken to increase their awareness of India's cultural heritage and history.
Adolescents need particular attention and concentrated efforts are required to build a relatively stable place in society
for them and help them overcome the barriers to healthy development.
Efforts will be made for networking between Government and non-Government Organi­sations (NGOs) in youth
development.”
            The Committee feels that the objectives are laudable.  However, unless dedicated and sincere efforts are
made to achieve these objectives they will remain on paper only. These objectives cannot be achieved overnight.
Rather, ground should have been prepared much earlier for attainment of these objectives. To start with, the
Committee feels, that a nationwide Yoga programme should be started under the supervision of trained
volunteers in a morning hour say between 5.00 to 6.00 a.m. as already mentioned in the foregoing paragraphs, in
order to harness the energies of youth.  The Committee hopes that efforts would commence in right earnest. This
is expected to energise the nation and also help promote unity.
V         YOUTH AFFAIRS PROGRAMMES
5.1       The total allocation made for Youth Affairs for the year 2003-2004  is Rs136.54 crores. This amount includes
Rs.109.23 crores on Plan side and Rs. 27.31 crores on Non-Plan side.  The entire Budgetary allocation consists of Rs.
122.54 crores - Rs. 95.23 crores (Plan) and Rs. 27.31 crores (Non-Plan) made last year. Though the allocation on Plan
side this year has been increased by about Rs.14 crores, the Committee feels that the overall annual plan allocation is
not sufficient keeping in view the schemes being implemented by the Ministry and the objectives that have been set
forth in the Tenth plan document.   More so, the inflation pressure and the increasing youth population in the country are
likely to make things more difficult.

141thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report141th.htm[01-07-2016 16:19:47]
The Committee observes that there is an urgent need to address the existing scenario of youth problems which is
reflected in the unlawful activities of misguided youth of the country. Youth power, if directed properly, can change the
socio-economic scenario of the country.  Added to this lack of adequate employment opportunities, lack of direction
because of uncertain education system, inability to pursue education because of financial constraints are compelling
youth to take to the crimes to find some easy money to sustain life.   In these circumstances, the Committee is
constrained to note that the achievement of targets, both financial and physical, by the youth wing has not been
satisfactory.  Infact the budgetary support  during Ninth Five Year Plan remained unutilized.   Against the approved
outlay of was Rs.352.24 crores for the Ninth Plan expenditure incurred amounted to  Rs.336.94 crores.   The Committee
agrees with the view expressed by the Approach Paper to the Ninth Plan that the social sector programmes have not
performed upto the mark.   The Committee is therefore of the view that the monitoring and evaluation system either
does not exist and even if it exists, the findings of it are not being seriously taken. These are the reasons due to which
the targets could not be achieved on both financial and physical fronts. 
The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry should tighten and strengthen its monitoring system to
ensure achievement of targets.  Two Vital factors like inflation, increasing number of youth and paramount need
to channelise the  energies of youth in right direction be kept constantly in view while making allocations to the
Department.
            On being asked that though the country has one billion people, what were the reasons for performing badly in
International events, the Ministry stated that India was the most populous country in the world after China. But our
sports playing population was very less.  It is estimated that out of one billion, only a few lakhs pursue sports for
recreation and even fewer for participation in competitive sports. Quality comes out of quantity and with a narrow base
of sports playing population especially for competitive sports; it was very difficult to find adequate number of athletes
of international level. Unlike China, the role and contribution of educational institutions/universities to Indian sports is
quite meagre.  Apart from lack of sports culture, the country also lacked the kind of resources necessary for achieving
excellence in sports. India being a developing country, limited budgetary resources were allocated for sports activities.
Efforts were being made to bridge the gap in resources by involving the private sector and getting assistance from some
public sector undertakings of some Central Ministries such as the Ministry of Coal.
            The Committee feels that in order to promote Sports in the country it is necessary to provide adequate
incentives, good job opportunities and recognition of talent and achievements through an independent
assessment and honest promotion of sports.  At the same time while it is desirable to enlist cooperation of private
sector, it may not be forthcoming unless this is linked to tax incentives.
VI        NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN (NYKS)
6.1       Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan was a Central autonomous body of the Ministry which has Nehru Yuva Kendras
in the districts functioning under it. It is one of the largest grass root level organizations in Asia-Pacific region, catering
to more than 8 million youth in the age group of 15-35 years. This organization was working for giving extra thrust to
the activities of non-student rural youth through programmes such as youth leadership, training, community service
programmes, vocational training, sports and recreation, cultural activities, non-formal education, etc.
6.2       NYKS accomplished its task through two categories of programmes i.e. Regular Programmes and Special
Programmes.  Plan Financial outlay made under this scheme was to the tune of Rs. 31.18 crores for the current year as
against a provision of Rs. 28.38 crores last year.  It has been stated that the marginal increase of Rs.2.80 crores was
necessitated on account of  the requirement of payment of arrears to the employees of Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan
who have been placed in  higher scales of pay, in terms of  the scheme of Assured Career Progression.    B.E. 2001-2002
and 2002-2003 provided enhanced allocation as compared to earlier years due to the sanction of a new project for self
employment of Youth and normal increase of expenditure necessitated by   inflationary pressures in the economy. 
The  Committee feels that the activities/programmes undertaken by NYKS were good in promoting communal
harmony but they hardly reach the grassroot levels.  Lack of awareness among people deprived them to fully
exploit the benefits of the programme.   The Committee,  therefore, feels that it is necessary to give wide publicity
to the activities of NYKS to invite increased participation.
Nevertheless, the achievements by NYKS under various schemes during the entire Ninth Plan period viz. number of
programmes, Financial Assistance for Promotion of Youth Activities and Training National Service Volunteer Scheme
and Assistance to Youth Clubs have been quite encouraging.
VII      NATIONAL SERVICE SCHEME (NSS)
7.1       The scheme started in 1969-70 was being implemented through universities, colleges and other institutions of
higher learning. Expenditure on the scheme was shared on 7:5 basis between the Govt. of India and the States except in
case of Govt. of J&K and UTs without legislatures where the entire expenditure was met by the Central Govt. The

141thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report141th.htm[01-07-2016 16:19:47]
Scheme has two types of programmes, viz. "Regular Activities" and "Special Camping programmes" undertaken by its
volunteers. Under "Regular Activities", students were expected to work as volunteers for a continuous period of two
years, rendering community service for a minimum of 120 hours per annum. The activities included improvement of
campuses, tree plantation, constructive work in adopted villages and slums, work in welfare institutions, blood donation,
adult and non-formal education, health, nutrition, family welfare, AIDS awareness campaign, etc. Under "Special
Camping Programme", Camp of 10 days' duration was conducted every year in the adopted areas on specific themes
like "Youth for afforestation and Tree Plantations", "Youth for Rural Reconstruction", "Youth for Development",
"Youth for Mass Literacy", "Youth for Sustainable Development (with focus on wasteland Development)" and
"Watershed Management" in the New Millennium, the NSS theme for Special Camping was 'Youth for Healthy
Society" which was being launched from the year 1999.  The theme chosen for the year 2003-2004 is "Swacchta"
(Cleanliness).   These programmes provided ample opportunities to the students for group-living, collective experience
sharing and constant interaction with different communities. Adoption of a village/area was also one of the meaningful
programmes undertaken by the NSS Volunteers.  Village adoption programme ensured continuity of work, vis.-a-vis.,
sustained action, evaluation and follow up work.
NSS has over 19 lakh student volunteers spread over 176 Universities and 22 Senior Secondary Councils. From its
inception, more than 2.51 crore students from universities, colleges and institutions of higher learning have benefitted
from NSS activities.
A target of 9500, each,  for Adoption of Villages and Special Camping Programmes has been fixed for the year 2003-04
. The identification of villages for adoption and camp sites has been done at the unit level i.e. +2 School, college and
university having NSS units.
The activities of the NSS network would be expanded to cover all degree colleges and +2 schools while the NRC would
extend its reach to 500 districts by the end of the Tenth Plan period because  it is felt that because all categories of
youth, including rural youth, should get an opportunity to participate in various schemes like the National Cadet Corps
(NCC), NSS, Scouts and Guides and NRC.
            The Committee observes it is necessary to have another look on the three-tier system to determine the extent to
which it has helped.  The Committee notes that the utilisation of allocated funds under NSS continues to be the
optimum.  The Committee is surprised to learn how in the absence of Audited Accounts/utilisation certificates,
allocation of funds has been continuing for years together.
 The Committee, therefore, is of the view that before going for enhancement in the scale of assistance for regular
activities and special camps under NSS, it is necessary to develop an effective monitoring system to curb the
misuse of expenditure, if any.
7.2       Ministry submitted that the Plan allocation has been kept at the same level of Rs.23.40 crores in B.E., R.E. 2002-
2003 and the 2003-2004 on account of accumulation of unspent balances lying with several States/UTs and non-
submission of audited accounts by the State Governments/U.T. Administrations in time.

VIII     NATIONAL SERVICE VOLUNTEER SCHEME
8.1       The objective of the scheme is to provide opportunities to students, generally speaking, those who have
completed their graduation, to involve themselves, on a voluntary basis, in nation-building activities for a specific
period on a whole time basis. Any person, who has completed his/her degree course and is below 25 years of age may
get himself/herself enrolled as a National Service Volunteer for one/two years. The requirement of age and educational
qualification is relaxable in case of SC/ST and women volunteers. Each of the volunteers enrolled under the scheme, is
paid a stipend of Rs. 1000/- per month. The number of National Service Volunteers sanctioned during the year 2002-03,
is 4700. Apart from the Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, the beneficiaries include the National Service Scheme, Bharat

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
While the role and contribution of youth is of vital importance in all countries, it is particularly significant in a
country like India where the proportion of the youth in the country’s overall social and demographic profile is
continuously increasing. According to the 2001 Census, there were approximately 355 million people in the 15 to
35 age group, 74 per cent of whom lived in rural areas. The number was expected to rise to approximately 510
million by 2016. Both central and state governments need to harness the energies of this large group, providing
them with adequate infrastructure of world standards for excellence in sports at national and international
levels.
The Committee is constrained to observe that no organized effort appears to be forthcoming over a national scale to tap
the potential of the Youth. Youth are the foundation for the development of the country and unless emphasis is laid on
youth programme and put the youth on the right track and right direction, the ultimate goal of nation building can not be
achieved.  The Committee feels that in order to develop the youth, a yoga programme should be started throughout the
country for different age groups with a definite capsule of different sets of exercises provided for different age groups. It
should be as near to the homes of the people as possible. Adequate number of volunteers should be trained for the
purpose who may conduct the exercises in Yoga suited to different age groups. These exercises may be conducted in an
hour say between 5 to 6 a.m. throughout the country. It should be designated a national hour. The trained volunteers
may be paid an allowance for the purpose. This would infuse new energy & fitness among the people and help build a
strong nation. Further modalities, if any, could be worked out. The services of any existing organization could also be
utilized for the purpose. (Para 2.2)
APPROACH TO THE TENTH FIVE YEAR PLAN
The Committee feels that the objectives are laudable.  However, unless dedicated and sincere efforts are made to
achieve these objectives they will remain on paper only. These objectives cannot be achieved overnight. Rather,
ground should have been prepared much earlier for attainment of these objectives. To start with, the Committee
feels, that a nationwide Yoga programme should be started under the supervision of trained volunteers in a
morning hour say between 5.00 to 6.00 a.m. as already mentioned in the foregoing paragraphs, in order to
harness the energies of youth.  The Committee hopes that efforts would commence in right earnest. This is
expected to energise the nation and also help promote unity. (Para 4)
YOUTH AFFAIRS PROGRAMMES
            The Committee feels that in order to promote Sports in the country it is necessary to provide adequate
incentives, good job opportunities and recognition of talent and achievements through an independent
assessment and honest promotion of sports.  At the same time while it is desirable to enlist cooperation of private
sector, it may not be forthcoming unless this is linked to tax incentives. (Para 5)
NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN (NYKS)
The  Committee feels that the activities/programmes undertaken by NYKS were good in promoting communal
harmony but they hardly reach the grass root levels.  Lack of awareness among people deprived them to fully
exploit the benefits of the programme.   The Committee, therefore, feels that it is necessary to give wide publicity
to the activities of NYKS to invite increased participation. (Para 6.2)
NATIONAL SERVICE SCHEME
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should realize the importance of sports and take necessary steps
towards utilization of vast potential manpower of students gainfully either in sports or in completion of projects
of national importance during holidays in forms other than NCC camps.  If dedicated efforts are made, the
country can go a long way in bringing about a change in the sports scenario. (Para 7.3)
The Committee also recommends that purposeful activity should be taken in these camps to prove the theme of
NSS i.e. "Development of the Personality of the Students through Community".    Besides Programmes under

141thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report141th.htm[01-07-2016 16:19:47]
NSS should be constantly reviewed with a view to develop the  personality and promote meaningful interaction
among students. (Para 7.3)
NATIONAL INTEGRATION PROGRAMME
            The Committee feels that programmes of interest to the youth be devised with a view to promoting
community living and sharing of common experiences. (Para 9.3
YOUTH HOSTELS
            The Committee feels  it is necessary to give wide publicity to the existence of youth hostels and also
indicate therein the  requirement, if any, the youth were expected to fulfil for  making use of these youth hostels.
(Para 10)
YOUTH WELFARE ACTIVITIES
The Committee is aware that adolescents have special and distinct needs.  The most important issues concerning 
this segment of youth i.e. adolescents are: health, nutrition, education, both formal and non formal, vocation,
recreation and sports, child labour, children in difficult situations, alcohol and drug abuse.  The Committee
hopes that the Scheme would be implemented in letter and spirit within a stipulated timeframe keeping in view
the requirements related to this age group. (Para 11.3)
SPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA (SAI)
The Committee observes that SAI is required to be a purely professional entity devoid of bureaucratic control
and solely devoted to its objective of promoting sports so that country finds an honored place in the comity of
nations.  (Para 12.3)
To that end, among other things, the Committee observes that it is absolutely necessary that there is not only
adequate infrastructure in the matter of sports and also whatever infrastructure is created it should be of
international standard.  Besides, it is equally necessary to maintain it and providing timely renewals, repairs and
replacements which is generally not forthcoming.  (Para 12.3)
GRANT TO NATIONAL SPORTS FEDERATIONS
The Committee observes that the entire structure be it the creation of infrastructure, role of sports federations 
in the promotion of sports, selection of sportspersons  for national as well as international events smacks of
favoritism and not free from  corruption.  Even the role of sports federations does not seem to be objective.  The
Committee has been given to understand that there are cases where sports federation are in existence for name
sake and for receiving grants.  They are not concerned with the promotion of sports.  The Committee would like
to go into their working later.  (Para 13.3)
RURAL SPORTS PROGRAMME
The Committee recommends that Sports activities need to be encouraged keeping in mind the facilities available,
particularly in rural areas and the need to keep in youth fit and keep them engaged in sports activities. As far as
possible, disci­plines which did not require much equipment such as kho-kho, kabaddi, volleyball, track events
and long jump in athletics should be encouraged. Efforts should also be made to enlist the cooperation of  the
Ministry of Rural Development in the promotion of sports in rural areas. The Ministry should extend assistance
to the panchayats for the creation and maintenance of play fields and for providing sports equipment. (Para 14)
 SPECIAL AREA GAMES (SAG)
   The Committee recommends that efforts should also be made to tap potential for swimming in coastal areas,
and archery in tribal areas.(Para 15.2)
 ALL INDIA COUNCIL FOR PHYSICAL EDUCATION
The Committee welcomes the move of the Ministry for setting up a body of national stature and hopes that the
Council would fulfil the objects  for which it is proposed to be set up.  However, the Committee hopes that the
proposed council would not be a mere addition to the existing institutions and would  be a specialised body
professionally devoted to its objectives. (Para 16.2) 
 AFRO – ASIAN GAMES
            The Committee recommends that everything possible should be done to ensures that the games/events are
conducted successfully and no inconvenience is caused to visiting teams/delegations and the event goes down the
memory as a successful event.  Govt. should also try to have the dope test center duly accredited from IOC well
before the games start.          (Para 17.2)
 INCENTIVES FOR PROMOTION OF SPORTS ACTIVITIES/EVENTS
            The Committee was given to understand that National Welfare Fund for sportpersons was meant to
provide assistance to sportspersons living in indigent circumstances.  However,  it remained a fact that some of
our former sportpersons lived in abject poverty and were sometimes forced to do odd jobs, in order to eke a

141thReportofHRD

living.  Except in cases of  a few popular sports, which attracted private sponsorship, the sports activities
remained devoid of any career opportunities for sportspersons. The Committee feels that  there is a need to have
definite incentives for sportspersons in the form of job opportunities. (Para 18.2)
 GRANTS FOR CREATION OF SPORTS INFRASTRUCTURE
The Committee reiterates the need for creation of adequate infrastructure and that too of an international
standard.  This should be thrown open to all and sundry individuals as well as groups on moderate charges.  This
would facilities the encouragement of sports.  (Para 19.2)
             After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Family Welfare and assessing the
progress of various programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands
for Grants of Rs. 4954.52 crores as sought by the Department of Family Welfare for the year 2003-2004, under
Demand No.48 may be approved. (Para 20)

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE
BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
I           INTRODUCTION
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Immunisation Status (% coverage) has considerably gone up in
2001-02 as compared to 1985-86 in respect of pregnant women as also infants. The Committee recommends this tempo
may be maintained with a view to ensure cent percent coverage.
 
Action Taken
 
            The Department has noted the observations of the Committee.
 
A number of measures like replacement of ageing cold chain equipment, training of district level managers,
preparation of micro plans for routine immunisation, improved monitoring and supervision are being undertaken in
order to improve and sustain the quality and coverage of the immunisation programme.
 
V         REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH (RCH) PROGRAMME
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
Although in BE 2003-04, the higher allocation of funds have been provided than that of RE 2002-03 but it is still
less than that of BE 2002-03. The Committee hopes that again at RE stage during this financial year, the allocation may
not be curtailed like previous year due to the same reasons. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should take steps in right earnest and utilize the entire allocation effectively without any lacklustre attitude.
 
Action Taken
 
The Department agrees with the observations of the Committee about not curtailing the outlay of these
programmes at RE stage. All efforts will be made to utilize the entire allocation effectively, as recommended by the
Committee.
 
V         Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee notes that out of 17 States, 9 States actively organizing RCH camps have shown positive results

142nd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/142ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:20]
in those States. The Committee recommends that efforts should be made to pursue the remaining State Governments
where the RCH camps could not be held and efforts should be made to cover maximum number of districts in these
States.
 
Action Taken
 
 The scheme of providing RCH services to people living in remote areas through RCH camps has been initiated
during the year 2000-01.   Initially 102 districts in 17 States were selected for implementation of the scheme.   Later,
based on the reports received from the State Governments, the scheme was extended to 76 more districts, which are now
spread in 29 States.   These include all the EAG States namely Bihar, Jharkhand, UP, Uttranchal, Madhya Pradesh,
Chhatisgarh, Rajasthan and Orissa and all the NE States. It has been decided to extend the scheme in all the districts of
EAG and NE States. The States have been requested to reflect the requirement in their State Action Plan.
 
A total of 4633 camps have been held as reported. The Government of India has so far released a sum of Rs.
16.97 crores for this scheme. In the year 2002-03, a sum of Rs. 2.92 crores had been released.  While detailed guidelines
have been circulated to all the States/UTs for implementation of the Scheme, States have also been pursued to hold the
camps regularly in selected PHCs as per the guidelines of the programme, through various review meetings and
communications.
 
XIII
     AREA PROJECT
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee also notes that during the year 2000-01 and 2001-02, allocation at RE stage was reduced due to
reasons such as unspent balance lying with States. The Committee is not happy with the trend of utilization of the funds
and recommends that accounting procedure should be strengthened to check the practice of unspent balance.
 
Action Taken
 
To ensure proper utilization of funds, the utilization certificate of funds earlier released are invariably called for.
To check the practice of unspent balance, release of funds are now made only after taking into account the expenditure
incurred out of amount already released and after reviewing the physical and financial progress of the project from time
to time. The concerned State Governments are being informed about the concern of the Committee regarding slow
utilization of funds.
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE
IN VIEW OF GOVERNMENTS’ REPLY
IV        URBAN FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES (UFWS)
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee notes that the allocation under the scheme has marginally been increased from BE & RE of Rs.
109.80 crores to Rs. 119.50 crores in BE 2003-04. The actual expenditure figures were not available at the point of time.
The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to utilize the allocation judiciously as well as timely.
 
Action Taken
 
The figure indicated in the Report relates to the States and UTs other than NE States and Sikkim. The
corresponding actual expenditure during the year 2002-2003 was Rs. 101.60 crores.  An amount of Rs. 6.97 crore
earmarked for Delhi could not be released due to non-submission of audited statement of accounts by Delhi
Government.
 

142nd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/142ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:20]
            The Department has noted the comments of the Committee. Every effort will be made to utilize the allocation
judiciously.
 
VIII
     TRANSPORT
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee observes that the impact of non-release of funds for providing transport to ANMs and others be
assessed and the scheme reconsidered in light of this assessment for reintroduction with such modifications as are
considered necessary.
 
Action Taken
 
As regards Moped Loan Scheme for purchase of mopeds for ANMs in order to increase their mobility, its initial
implementation was with UNFPA assistance.   Under the scheme, a fixed amount of Rs.16000/- was to be given to the
ANMs as loan that was to be returned without interest to the State Governments. During the year 2000-01, an amount of
Rs.84.57 lakhs was released for the purpose.   
 
However, this one time support from UNFPA is not available any more. Though the scheme continues to be a
part of RCH Programme of the Department, its strengthening is proposed in the RCH-II Project. In it, it is envisaged
that the Government of India will release funds for being used by the State Governments for extending loans to ANMs
for procurement of mopeds to increase their mobility. There will be no interest subsidy from Government of India.  The
State Governments will work out the list of remote PHCs (a remote PHC should be at least 10 Km. away from a District
and Sub-divisional headquarters) and, therefore, the number of ANMs eligible for such loans should not exceed more
than 25% of the total ANMs in the State.   On the basis of such number, the State Government will request the
requirement of funds to the Central Government.   The nationalized banks or State Cooperative banks will make the
arrangements for receiving the money from Government of India and put it in the Corpus Fund out of which loans will
be sanctioned by their branches to the ANMs.   The number of ANMs to be covered, the size of Corpus Fund required,
the decision to provide interest subsidy and copy of the MOU finalized with the bank will have to be furnished to the
Government of India for securing release of funds for the purpose.
           
After the ANMs in the identified remote PHCs would have been covered, the recovery of loan from these ANMs
will be utilized for extending loan to other ANMs and para-medical employees of the State Health & Family Welfare
Department.
 
IX 
       COMPENSATION
 
Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee notes the enhancement in the amount of compensation and recommends a review thereof after making a
realistic assessment of cost of inputs thereunder such as diets, transport and drugs and dressings etc., and also the
component of payment to motivator.
 
Action Taken
 
The government is providing assistance to the States/UTs to compensate the people for the loss of wages for the
days they come to the medical centre for permanent or temporary methods of family planning. The Government has
modified the scheme of cash compensation for sterilisation/IUD insertion w.e.f. 7th February 2001.
 
Regarding the review of the cash compensation, it is mentioned here that norms of compensation for sterilisation/
IUD insertion were revised very recently, with effect from 7.2.2001. However, the Department is considering its
revision at the time of implementation of RCH-II Project, which is likely to be taken up from next financial year.
 

142nd Report of HRD

X         INFORMATION, EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION (IEC)
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee is happy to note the steps taken by the Department. However, it appears that the people in
villages and remote areas may not be reached until and unless intensive advertising is forthcoming. The Committee feels
that the possibility  of involvement of local administration and representatives of local people for these programmes
should also be explored.
Action Taken
 
IEC activities are carried out to achieve wider publicity of the RCH and population stabilization programme by
respective Mass Education and Media Set-up created in the States and through Media Units of the Ministry of
Information and Broadcasting.
 
The Department, with the enhanced allocation in BE 2003-04, will carry out the intensive IEC activities in 8
EAG States; enhanced publicity through print and electronic media, viz, printing of immunisation cards and booklets
through Directorate of Advertising and Visual Publicity (DAVP); and upgraded publicity for Pulse Polio Immunisation
Programme on Doordarshan & All India Radio.

health.

for creating audio visual and visual software and for designing advertising campaigns for the Mass Media have been

sensitization workshops at State/Dist./PHC and Block level involving local people of repute, MLAs, elected

village level Swasthya committees are also being mobilized.

Recommendation/Observation

The Committee notes that there have been marginal fluctuations in the case of contraceptive methods at certain
point of time. Nevertheless, the Committee feels satisfied that the concept of family planning has at last been accepted
and has become a part of family life. The Committee recommends that the awareness programme in this respect should
continue so that the apprehensions of general public about the usage of contraceptives are allayed.
 
Action Taken
 
Awareness generation activities are being taken up through the mass media, both electronic and print. Efforts
will continue to be made to achieve the maximum population coverage. A national Commitment for Population
Stabilisation is being launched through a signature campaign throughout the country to create awareness in all age
group.
 
Comments of the Committee
Despite the efforts made by the Department to create awareness about the usage of contraceptives,   it appears to
be far from reality, as the desired  results are not foreseen. The Department should hire the services of Advertising
Agencies to create mass awareness specially in rural areas through intensive advertising.    Besides this, the involvement
of office bearers of village Panchayats and other local bodies should also be explored so that the message is
communicated effectively at every level specially in  remote areas.
II 
        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
While the Committee appreciates the constraints of budgetary exercise of matching the known resources of
revenue with the requirements of outflow of funds, it expresses its concern over huge cut in the allocation. We are
already seized of the effects of over population. Family Planning as well as Welfare are, therefore, unavoidable vital
component of the Planning in our country. Abdication of responsibility by way of non-allocation is fraught with
disastrous consequences. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Planning Commission should review the
allocation and provide additional funds at the earliest so that continuity of welfare programmes and schemes is ensured
so that it does not affect the pace of steps being taken to right-size the population of the country.
 
Action Taken
 
            The Planning Commission has replied that it has made every effort to provide the Department of Family Welfare
as much outlay as possible within the existing financial constraints during Annual Plan 2003-04. The total increase in
Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) provided for Annual Plan 2003-04 is Rs.7474 crores for both Central and State Plans.
Keeping in view the commitments and policy announcement of the Government, only the sectors identified for special
thrust like power, railways, road transport and atomic energy & space etc. have been given marginal increase. Budget
allocations to all other Central Ministries and Departments have been frozen at the BE level of 2002-03. Although the
GBS for Annual Plan 2003-04 of the Department of Family Welfare has been kept at the BE level of 2002-03 (Rs.4930
crores), it is higher by 18.8 % than the RE of Rs.4150 crores for the year 2002-03.
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is baffled to know that the Planning Commission does not consider the family welfare, whose
basic mandate is to control the population, as special thrust area. Population, in fact, neutralizes the fruits of
development and reduces the per capita availability of resources. Population control, therefore, has to have equal
emphasis as is being given to areas like power, railways, road transport, etc.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates that
the Planning Commission may be requested to keep this fact in mind and raise the budgetary allocation for the
Department during the next financial year.

Recommendations/Observation

PHCs/CHCs/FRU/District Hospitals etc., it can assess the plight of these units based on the grossly inadequate and poor

that steps should continue to be taken to strengthen these units to provide maximum health care facilities as also in
terms of man power.
 
Action Taken
 
            To strengthen health care infrastructure, Government of India is assisting all the States in improving/constructing
labour rooms and operation theatres and in providing water/electricity supply in CHCs/PHCs etc. so that essential and
emergency obstetric services are improved. Under Minor Civil Works Scheme, an amount of Rs.10 lakhs per district has
been provided (one time release). Under Major Civil Works Scheme, an amount of Rs.10 lakhs per CHC/District
Hospital is being provided.
 
            The Government of India provides funds for Sub-Centres but filling up of the vacancies and transfer & posting
of the concerned staff lies totally under the control of State Government. However, Director, Health Services of all
States have been requested time & again for filling up the vacancies at various levels.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
India has shown significant improvement in the area of health and well being of its people.  But the Committee
feels that we are still not fully equipped in the area of health management, including quality of care. The facilities at
CHC/PHCs are still not adequate enough to meet the challenges of new kind of diseases, which are erupting in various
parts of the country now and then. In the absence of poor facilities in the Rural and Urban Health Centres, the load in
the Hospitals in the Metros and bigger cities has increased tremendously resulting in the available services going
haywires.
 
The Department has informed that the filling of vacancies and posting of medical officials in the PHC/CHCs

should not sit as mute spectator as it is supporting the States in a big way for extending /improving health and family
welfare services for these people.   Therefore, the Centre must persuade them effectively for filling up the posts lying
vacant for a long time.  It may link release of funds by it with this aspect.

VII      STRENGTHENING OF IMMUNISATION PROGRAMME AND ERADICATION OF POLIO
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
Keeping in view the importance of this scheme, the Committee observes that it was unwise to reduce the
allocation of funds for this scheme at RE stage.
 
The Committee notes with concern the number of polio cases detected in 1998, 1999, 2000, 2001 and 2002.

The Committee observes that in matters of health and that too of the children even a single such case would
suffice to send wrong signals among people about the scheme. The Department should, therefore, create awareness
among general masses about the benefits of the Scheme and ensure that no child is left uncovered under immunisation
programme. At the same time the Committee recommends that no cuts should hereafter be made in such schemes.
 
Action Taken
 
 Since the initiative to eradicate polio from India was started in 1995, significant progress was achieved by the
end of 2001 in limiting the spread of virus to certain foci in the western and central UP and Bihar only. The number of
polio cases declined from 1934 in 1998 to 1128 in 1999, 265 in 2000 and 268 in 2001. At that stage, it was anticipated
that by the end of the year 2002, it would be possible to eradicate the virus from the remaining reservoirs in UP and
Bihar. However, during 2002, the polio eradication effort in India suffered a major setback due to large-scale outbreak
in UP and spill over into other neighboring States, and the number of cases sharply increased from 268 to 1600. India,
which reported around 37% of the global cases in 2000, reported 83% of the global cases during 2002. During 2001, 11
States had reported 268 cases across 63 districts. During 2002, 1600 cases have been reported from 16 States and 169
districts. In view of the seriousness of the situation and in order to interrupt the transmission of virus, the Government is
actively considering implementation of two National Immunization Days (NIDs) and four Sub-national Immunization
Days (SNIDs) in continuation of the January and February, 2003 rounds (which have already been conducted) so that
the gains of the January and February 2003 national rounds could be consolidated in the high risk States/districts
through these additional rounds.
 
The social mobilization and IEC activities have been significantly improved and local areas of rumours and
misconceptions are being addressed with the focus that not a single child is missed during the ensuing rounds.

XI        TRAINING, RESEARCH AND EVALUATION
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
While the Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Department, it recommends that adequate
monitoring mechanism and accounting procedure should be provided for running the scheme. Utilization Certificates
and Statement of Expenditure should be obtained quarterly and reviewed. However, the Committee observes that for the
purpose of Family Welfare Programme in the country, the schemes are in abundance but the basic problem with all the
schemes is that they lack in appropriate strategy in implementing the schemes. This scheme was formulated almost two
decades back but no one ever thought of its effective implementation.
 
Action Taken
This Head of Training, Research & Evaluation consists of the 13 Schemes. The major schemes being ‘Basic
Training for ANMs/LHVs’, ‘Maintenance & Strengthening of HFWTCs’,  ‘Basic Training for MPWs (Male)’,
‘Strengthening of Basic Training Schools’, ‘ICMR’, ‘Population Research Centres’, ‘NIHFW’ and ‘IIPS’. Except
‘Strengthening of Basic Training Schools’, all the other schemes are old schemes and are functioning effectively.
During the Tenth Five Year Plan, the scheme ‘Strengthening of Basic Training Schools’ envisages to strengthen the
ANM/LHV Training Schools in terms of repair/upgradation of the buildings of training centres and procuring furniture,
equipments, books, audio-visual aids for conducting training. This initiative has been taken to improve the infrastructure
in the Schools for Basic Training of ANMs/LHVs. The SFC proposal for this scheme has been prepared. The appraisal
of Planning Commission has also been obtained. After approval of the scheme, the releases will be made based on the
merit of each proposal, forwarded by the State Governments. The State Governments will be instructed regarding
periodical submission of UCs/SOEs.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee reiterates that there are plethora of Schemes, but not all of these were being implemented
effectively for various reasons.  Lack of adequate monitoring and effective accounting procedures is one of these
causes.  The Committee recommends that a comprehensive evaluation/review of all these schemes be done with a view
to evolving appropriate strategies for their implementation.

XV       NEW INITIATIVES NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY 2000
Recommendations/Observation
The Committee feels that the problem of exponential growth of the population is the mother of all the problem in
the country which would have an impact on economic needs of the people irrespective of the growth rate of national
economy. However, the Committee is of the view that the population explosion in the country has not received adequate
attention. In fact, the problem should have been tackled on a war footing. Nevertheless, the Committee feels that instead
of producing coercion in family planning, a system of incentives be introduced where under the families with one or two
children may be given preferences in various types of services e.g. telephone connection, railway reservation, admission
of children to schools including public schools so on and so forth, in order to send a clear message of preference and a
place of pride to small families.
 
Action Taken
            The Government has adopted the National Population Policy (NPP) in February 2000, which envisages certain
National Socio-demographic goals to be achieved by 2010 for paving the way for a stable population in the country by
2045, at a level consistent with the requirements of sustainable economic growth and social development. It provides a
policy framework for advancing goals and prioritizing strategies during the next decade, to meet the reproductive and
child health needs of the people of India, and to achieve net replacement levels (TFR = 2.1) by 2010. Before finalizing
the NPP, the drafts were discussed repeatedly by the Group of Ministers. However, there was no unanimity on inclusion
of personal incentives or disincentives. Accordingly, no mention was made of these in the NPP-2000.
 
However, certain promotional/motivational measures in the form community incentives, cash incentive of Rs.
500/- under the Balika Samridhi Yojana, National Maternity Benefit Scheme etc. have been introduced to encourage the
adoption of small family norm, care of the girl child, adoption of healthy behaviour by women during pregnancy, etc.
 
The Government proposes to launch a Janani Suraksha Yojana under which cash support of Rs. 500/- will be
given for birth of male child and Rs.1000/- for birth of female child upto two live births to all women aged 19 years or
above belonging to below poverty line (BPL) household in both rural and urban area. After two children, if any pregnant
woman chooses for permanent contraception, she will also be eligible for the above assistance under the scheme. A
assistance of Rs. 150/- shall be given for transportation to hospital for delivery. In case the trained birth attendant (Dai)
has been instrumental in taking a pregnant woman to a Primary Health Centre/Hospital for delivery, she will also be
paid Rs. 25/-.

142nd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/142ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:20]
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee feels that the amount of incentives given for adopting small family norms is not adequate
enough to encourage people to adopt these norms vigorously. Enhancing these incentives to appropriate extent should
be considered, as the present incentives have not attracted people towards adopting small family norms.
 
XVI     NUTRITIONAL ANAEMIA CONTROL PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
            The Committee recommends that such corrective steps be taken to ascertain the reasons behind this condition
and if necessary an extension survey be considered to unfold the hidden problem.
 
Action Taken
To improve nutritional status of pregnant women, in addition to distribution of IFA tablets among all pregnant
women, feasibility of introducing herbal/Ayurvedic formulations is being planned. Studies in India and abroad indicate
that introduction of de-worming in the 2 nd/3rd trimester of pregnancy may reduce the level of anemia. However, wider
consultation in this regard would be essential before introduction of this treatment in the National Programme.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee notes the reply furnished by the Department. However, it feels that whatever consultation/
experiment/study/research is required to introduce the treatment for improving the nutritional status of pregnant women
should be completed at war footing so that, nutritional anemia control programme may be made successful.   All sorts of
post treatment apprehensions should also be cleared out by media publicity.

contained in its One Hundred-Thirty Seventh Report on Demands for Grants (Demand No.47) of the Department of
Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2003-2004.
2.         Action Taken Notes received from the Government have been considered by the Committee have been
categorized as follows:-

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE
BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
 
II         STRATEGIES FOR 10th FIVE-YEAR PLAN
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
2.3       The Secretary of the Department informed the Committee that against the  BE for the 9
th  plan period of 
Rs.364.43 crore, RE Rs.317.8 crores; actual expenditure was Rs.293.71 crores.  Thus there was a short fall of Rs.70.72
crore and the reasons given for the short fall are as under-
-           Implementing agencies did not submit utilization certificates on time for availing 2nd subsequent installments;
-           States were slow in submitting proposals;
-           Whenever construction was involved,
-           Necessary civic clearances took a long time;
States gave low priority of ISM&H as compared to Health & Family Welfare
 
Action Taken
 
2.3       In order to monitor the expenditure of allotted budget, utilization of grants and submission of utilization
certificates (UCs) by the States/grantee institutions, a Monitoring Mechanism was evolved and a proforma has been
circulated to States for procuring monthly information on regular basis.   The objective is to persuade the States and
grantee institutions to utilize the funds in time and submit the Utilisation Certificate etc. so that fresh proposals could be
considered for sanction of grants. The monitoring is being done regularly. Achievement-cum-performance report in
every case of grant is being obtained to assess the impact of assistance given to a particular institution.  States especially
the North Eastern States are being repeatedly reminded.  All the pending Civic clearances for the Central Govt. Projects
have been obtained and the construction works started. A meeting of all the health secretaries of States was called on
31
st July and Ist August, 2003,  to sensitize them about the new Schemes besides getting feedback about the
implementation status  of the ongoing schemes.
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
2.5       The Committee feels that non submission of utilization certificates by the States is a perennial problem which is
derailing several developmental activities in the States.  The Committee is happy to note that Ministry of Finance has
formulated  guidelines on furnishing of utilisation certificates by the States. The Committee recommends that the
Department should constantly keep on hammering the states to submit utilization certificates and vigorously  implement
the Finance Ministry’s Guideline.
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department for the 10
th Plan.  However, the Committee, feels that unless
the causes for low utilization of funds as identified in the 9th  Plan are  addressed, the objectives of the 10th Plan may
not be fully realized.  As far as non submission of utilization certificates by the ‘Implementing Agencies’ is concerned,
the Committee feels that there could be possibilities of diversion, misutilisation or in some cases misappropriation of
Government funds. The Committee, therefore,  recommends that the Department should make an investigation as to
st

how the 1  Instalment of money has been utilized and fix responsibility in cases where  funds  have been  found to be
misappropriated .  The Committee is dismayed at the fact that most of the civic work required for the development of
the country gets trapped into labyrinths  of laws and by laws.  More laws means more beauracratization and more red
tape and thereby causing unnecessary postponement of or delay in implementing various developmental schemes.  The
Committee, therefore, feels that it is high time for the  Government including its various Department and Ministries to
put their head together, simplify the rules and procedures and also consider giving publicity to the schemes and
programmes aimed at the welfare of the People.
 
Action Taken
 
In the meeting of State Health Secretaries called on 31
st July and Ist August, 2003, the states were advised to
immediately submit all pending Utilization Certificates. The progress is being monitored regularly.  In some cases,
States have not released funds to the implementing agencies.  They have been repeatedly  impressed upon to implement
the schemes expeditiously to achieve the endresults and furnish Utilization Certificates.
The suggestions in this regard put forth by the Committee have been taken note of. Further, recently issued directions of
Ministry to pass on funds directly to implementing agencies will really help in expediting the pace of utilization of
funds.   All the old schemes of the department have recently been reviewed and the proforma etc simplified.  To ensure
wider publicity, activities including schemes of the Department have been put on internet in user friendly format. A
News Letter has also been started to publicize the activities of the Department.  To facilitate, formulation and
submission of good research project proposals, a workshop on research methodology was conducted by CCRAS.  All
the state holders were invited and guided.

allocation for the Department in BE 2002-2003 was Rs.150 crores which was reduced to Rs.105 crores   at the RE
stage.  The Department has  given `head-wise’ reduction in RE 2002-2003 as follows:

Explaining the reasons for reduction, the Department has informed  that  “this being the first year of the 10th Plan, a
number of new schemes were prepared for appraisal and approval, as required, of Planning Commission and
Department of  Expenditure for implementation during the 10th plan. However, the concurrence of Integrated Finance
Division, in-principle approval of Planning Commission, appraisal of Department of Expenditure, Plan Appraisal
Division of Planning Commission & clearance through EFCs and SFCs took a lot of time. Also, as a part of Zero Based
Budgeting(ZBB) exercise, all schemes were reviewed and regrouped by Planning Commission. This delayed the take
off of most of the schemes resulting in slow pace of expenditure and reduced RE.
 
Action Taken
 
3.1     By the time RE was finalized, the Schemes of the Department were at formulation stage and had not taken off. 
Therefore, a cut was imposed by Ministry of Finance.  Most of the schemes could take off only in the last quarter of the
year and therefore utilization of Rs.89 crore only could be done against RE of Rs.105 crore.  While delay in finalization
of New Schemes was one major reason for this gap between allocation and utilization, the lack of response from states,
the non furnishing of Utilization Certificates, non submission of proposals from North Eastern States and Sikkim, delay
in receipt of civic clearances in construction projects, non keeping of commitments by Contractors were other important
reasons.  Almost all schemes have now taken off and utilization is likely to improve this year.
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
3.2       The Committee is constrained to observe that in all the above mentioned 11 schemes, the allocation was reduced
at  RE stage. The Committee feels that prior to submitting its demands before Parliament, the Department should
conclude all necessary consultations with the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance and obtain their clearance
so that its budgetary allocation, once approved by  Parliament,  is not reduced subsequently.
 
Action Taken
 
3.2       This observation of the committee has also been noted for compliance in future. Due care will be taken to
complete all formalities prior to submitting its demands before Parliament.
 
IV.       PRACTICE OF INDIAN SYSTEMS OF MEDICINE AND HOMOEOPATHY IN PRIMARY HEALTH
CENTRES
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
4.1       The Committee is aware of the fact that the Primary Health Centers in general and particularly situated in remote
and far-flung areas are not functioning well. Doctors posted in such centers are either not inclined to accept rural posting
and if posted in a rural area, opt for an urban posting at the first available opportunity. As a result, majority of the
population of the Country which lives in rural areas are deprived of health services.
 
Action Taken
 
4.1       It is in this background that efforts are being made to post ISM&H doctors in PHCs of the States. However, the
states have to be adequately responsive to achieve the end results.
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
4.2       In reply to a question, the Secretary informed the Committee that the States of Himachal Pradesh, Tamil Nadu
and Kerala have posted ISMH doctors in their PHCs who have been assigned specific duties which are normally done
by the doctors of modern system.  In Himachal Pradesh, about 100 PHCs were without a doctor.  As  no allopathic
system doctor was willing to go there, the ISMH doctors were posted in such PHCs which resulted in increased
utilization of their services.  The Secretary further informed the Committee about a policy decision taken  some years 

143rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/143rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:21]
back that out of four posts, one post should be given to the ISMH doctors.  However, it is for the State Governments to
implement the decision.
 
Action Taken
 
4.2       The Department is pleading with State Governments in above mentioned line on all opportunities.
 
V.  AYURVEDA
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
5.2  The Plan allocation for Ayurveda in 2003-2004 is Rs.14.46 crores. The Committee has been informed that amongst
the European Countries only Hungary  has recognized the system of Ayurveda. Countries like, Russia, Italy, Spain,
Belgium, U.K. and U.S.A. though have shown keen interest for the system, are yet to recognize it.  These Countries,
though are positive about recognizing the system of Ayurveda but want assurance about the quality and safety of drugs. 
The Department has further informed that for ensuring quality control it has recently introduced good manufacturing
practices and laid down certain norms and standards for manufacture of Ayurvedic Medicine.
 
Action Taken
 
5.2       In the area of Drug standardization, following progress has been made:
Three volumes of Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of  India have been published and fourth volume is going to the press for
publication. So far 326 standard formulations on single drugs have been completed.
Two volumes of Ayurvedic Formulary of India containing 636 formulations have been published.
13 projects have been allotted to the various laboratories to develop Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) of
manufacturing processes and shelf life studies of compound Ayurvedic drugs.
17 State Drug Testing Laboratories for ISM drugs have been financed.
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
5.3   The Committee feels that the European Countries, USA and other developed and prosperous countries have
tremendous potential to become an extremely lucrative market for the Ayurvedic drugs of our country and can generate
a lot of foreign exchange for the Country. However, in order to achieve this, as rightly pointed out by the Department,
the confidence of such countries w.r.t. the safety and quality of such drugs has to be won. The Committee, therefore,
strongly recommends that the Department should keep a tight vigil of the quality and safety of the Ayurveda drugs
manufactured and used in India or exported out of India so that more and more countries recognize our traditional
system of medicine.
 
The Committee observes that people opt for traditional medicine because they are affordable and less harmful.
However, the experts have voiced concerns about the safety and quality, licensing of providers and standards of training
in connection with traditional medicines.
The World Health Organization has come out with a traditional medicine strategy for 2002-2005 which focuses on these
issues. According to WHO, 70 per cent of Indian population use traditional medicine for their primary health needs.
 
A group of experts recently met in Delhi to chalk out an adequate strategy for integration of traditional medicine with
the health care system in India. According to these experts, a set of standards for regulating traditional medicine and
setting up of a body to provide to medical claims is necessary.
The Committee feels the safety and efficiency of traditional medicine has been established through centuries of use.
However, in order to make it acceptable to the outside world it may be necessary to validate its scientific basis. Here,
the Committee is of the view that we need not tinker with our system for this purpose. Chernobyl incident convinced
Russians about the efficacy of our system of medicine when the victims’ burns were miraculously healed. Likewise
there are many simple plants and products like neem and turmeric, the efficacy of which tempted some countries abroad
to have these products patented for commercial exploitation. The Committee therefore reiterates that the system need
not be tinkered with to convince the outside world.

143rd Report of HRD

The attention of the Committee has been drawn to the fact that there are many traditional medicine practitioners who
have claimed a cure for some disease or the other. In most cases they end up making rounds of Government agencies or
try to sell their formula to pharmaceuticals but to little avail e.g. the person who claimed to have developed a herbal
contraceptive in the 1980, passed away by the time Government decided to follow it up. The Committee observes the
need to avoid such situations. The Government machinery should be suitably geared up and be responsive in such
situations.
 
Action Taken
 
5.3       The Department of Indian Systems of Medicines & Homoeopathy is committed to provide quality medicine to
the consumers. The National Policy of ISM&H 2002 envisages that:
Mostly Pharmacopoeial work related to Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy drugs would be completed by
2005. Enforcement mechanism will be activised.
Industry would be encouraged to make use of Quality Certification Scheme being introduced by the Department for
batch-by-batch testing.
Financial support would be given for acquisition of ISO 9000 certification by ISM industry.
 (d) New Legislation covering a vast range of nutraceuticals and food      supplements which are neither covered by the
drug licensing nor food licensing would be introduced
Quality Control Centres would be set up or recognized on a Regional basis to standardize the in process quality control
of ISM products and to modernize traditional processes without changing the concepts of ISM. States would be advised
to augment facilities for drug manufacture and testing of the drugs.
Drugs and Cosmetic Act would be amended to also cover grant of manufacturing licenses for intermediate or partially
processed herbal mixed and pharmacopoeial standards evolved for these intermediaries.
Towards achievement of these targets, the Department has implemented Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Quality
Control of Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani & Homoeopathy drugs. Under this scheme, there are 5 sub-schemes as follows:
Scheme for strengthening and establishment of State/U.T. Government Drug Manufacturing Pharmacies of ISM&H
drugs  (For State Govt.)
Scheme for strengthening enforcement mechanism for Quality Control of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani & Homoeopathy
drugs in states( for State Government).
Scheme for use of modern technology and bio-technology in Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani & Homoeopathy drugs
development ( for research institutions).
Scheme for assisting Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Drug manufacturing units to strengthen in-house Quality Control
section/DTL to meet the requirements of Good Manufacturing Practices(GMP) (for ISM drug manufacturers)
Scheme for assistance to Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani drug manufacturing units for obtaining Good Manufacturing
Practices(GMP) certification ( for ISM drug manufacturers).
 
Under the above scheme the Government have strengthened 17 State Drug Testing Laboratories and 32 Pharmacies of
ISM&H during the financial year 2002-2003. State DTL and Pharmacies have been approved by Project Selection
Committee (PSC) for giving assistance. In addition, Project Selection Committee (PSC) have approved for three states
i.e. Rajasthan, Punjab and Assam to strengthen their enforcement mechanism for Quality Control of Ayurveda, Siddha,
Unani and Homoeopathy drugs.
As far gearing up Government machinery to be responsive to the findings of traditional medicine practitioner, the
suggestion of the Committee has been noted for compliance.
 
YOGA AND NATUROPATHY
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
7.2       The Plan allocation for Yoga and Naturopathy for the year 2003-2004 is Rs.5.10 crores.  The Committee has
been informed that there are 6 colleges in the country which are imparting training in yoga and naturopathy and there is
also a Central Council for Yoga and Naturopathy which provides money for research and running of various schemes. 
The Secretary while deposing before the Committee informed that the Department of ISMH is planning to pass an Act
in the Parliament so as to empower the Council to grant recognition to the council so that Naturopathy and Yoga are

143rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/143rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:21]
regulated like other disciplines.
The Committee observes that the pros and cons should be considered before taking a decision to introduce legislation  in
this regard.
 
Action Taken
 
7.2   Keeping in view number of colleges imparting education and number of practitioners, it may not be possible to
enact a Central Act, for regulating education and practice of Yoga & Naturopathy for the present. However, as an
interim measure, steps have been initiated to authorize the Central Council for Research in Yoga & Naturopathy
(CCRYN), New Delhi to work out modalities for regulation of Yoga & Naturopathy education and practice.  As a long
term measure, the Central Government would enact a suitable legislation for establishing a Council for regulation of
Yoga & Naturopathy education and practice at an appropriate time. While enacting the legislation, thesuggestion of the
Committee will be kept in view.
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE
COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF GOVERNMENTS’ REPLY
 
VI        HOMOEOPATHY
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
6.2       Plan allocation for Homoeopathy was Rs. 10.21 crores in BE 2002-2003. However it has been reduced to Rs.
9.17 crores in BE 2003-2004. The Secretary while deposing before the Committee informed that presently there are 80
colleges of homoeopathy in the Country and out of which 17 colleges are imparting PG education.  However, there is no
separate university for Homoeopathy.
 
Action Taken
 
6.2       It is a matter of record.  There is no university of Homoeopathy, however, a National Institute of Homoeopathy
(N.I.H.) is already there.  It has been decided to upgrade it  into a Centre of Excellence, in the last Governing Body’s
meeting.  The action has been initiated.
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
6.3       The Committee feels that in the absence of a separate university, the Homoeopathy education is perhaps not
getting the attention it deserves. The Committee further feels that the quality of imparting Homoeopathy education can
be vastly improved if an exclusive Homoeopathy university is established to regulate and monitor the functioning of the
medical colleges throughout the Country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should consider
establishing a separate Homoeopathy University and the allocation under the head `Homoeopathy should be increased
accordingly.
 
At the same time there have been illiterate persons who acquired marvelous proficiency in developing this system of
medicine.  The Committee, therefore, feels that there should be room for persons with average qualification to study and
develop their skills in the field of Homoeopathy.  Part time colleges should also be encouraged to help people come
forward to acquire knowledge and expertise in this system of medicine.
 
Action Taken
 
6.3 The Central Council of Homoeopathy(CCH), New Delhi is set up under the Homoeopathic Central Council Act,
1973.  The objective of the CCH is to regulate the Homoeopathic practice and lay down the standards for Homoeopathic
education in the country. At present, we have 182 Under Graduate colleges and 31 Post-graduate colleges affiliated to
various Indian Universities.  In some of the States, a single University regulates the Homoeopathic teaching and
examination systems and in some of the States different regional Universities are taking care of the Homoepathic

143rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/143rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:21]
education. There is no separate Homoeopathic University in any State or under the Central Government.  However, the
suggestions of the Committee to have an exclusive Homoeopathic University has been noted.At present, the National
Institute of Homoeopathy is being upgraded from 60 bedded Hospital to 100 bedded Hospital and the plans are there to
make it a Centre of Excellence.
 
Since Homoeopathic education and practice is regulated through the Homoeopathic Central Council Act, 1973, part-
time course in Homoeopathy is not desirable in the opinion of experts of Homoeopathy.  Nevertheless, the suggestion of
Committee has been noted in this regard  too.
 
CHAPTER-III
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT
HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
 
II          STRATEGIES  FOR  10
th  FIVE  YEAR  PLAN
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
2.4       In order to deal with the problem of non-submission of utilization certificate by the States, the Secretary
informed that the only way to deal with this problem was to monitor the programme very strictly and persuade the State
Governments to submit the utilization certificates on time.  The Secretary further informed that the Finance Ministry
had recently come out with guidelines that the States which did not pass on the funds to the implementing agencies and
thereby causing delay in utilization of funds would be penalized.
 
Action Taken
 
2.4       Matter of record. However, recently, instructions have been received from the Finance Ministry that funds under
Centrally Sponsored Schemes can directly be released to implementing agencies.  This may ease situation in future.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE.
 
2.4       Main concern of the Committee has been the slow-utilisation of grants by the Department allocated for the
popularisation and development of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homeopathy and the Committee had been
reiterating this concern from time to time in its previous Reports.  To utter dismay of the Committee, the situation has
not improved despite the Government's claim of doing its best in this regard. The Committee is of the opinion that the

8.2       Quality Control of ISM&H drugs is one of the priority areas of the Department.  The Secretary informed the

8.3       It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that innumerable advertisements claiming that by using
